Source Material: Cambridge (UK) and Education

Cambridge fact file 2019
• Population: 124,800
• Percentage of population aged 18–29: 30%
• Percentage of people who cycle regularly: 54%
• Percentage of workers with a university qualification: 70%

Cambridge ranks number one amongst all UK cities in terms of the percentage of workers with a university qualification. It is also ranked number two in the UK in terms of the percentage of people aged 18–29. This is due to the high number of university students in Cambridge. Although the city has a relatively small population, its contribution to the overall size of the UK economy is significant.

Many firms in Cambridge operate in the education, healthcare, research and development, and hi-tech manufacturing industries. Cambridge firms' exports are highly knowledge-intensive, making them highly priced and price-inelastic in demand. Increasing global incomes have also increased the demand for services such as education from Cambridge.

The increase in the size of the education industry has the potential to reduce poverty. This is because a more educated labour force is able to earn higher wages and also have access to more information on health. Table 1.1 shows the percentage of population aged 25–64 with a university degree and the GDP per head in selected countries in 2019.

Table 1.1: % of population aged 25–64 with a university degree | GDP per head ($), 2019
• Canada: 57% | $46,195
• Colombia: 22% | $6,429
• Hungary: 24% | $16,732
• Indonesia: 12% | $4,136
• Switzerland: 43% | $81,994
• UK: 46% | $42,330

Many of the people who live in Cambridge are strong supporters of globalisation and free trade between countries. A large number of firms in Cambridge depend on export revenues.

Cambridge is an attractive location for growing firms because of the availability of many highly skilled and educated workers from all over the world. It has good infrastructure including access to ultra-fast broadband and transport links to other cities and international airports. However, firms may be faced with high land and office costs. In 2019, Cambridge was the city with the third highest house prices in the UK. Poor air quality may also discourage workers from moving to Cambridge.

The recent pandemic, however, reduced the revenues of many large and small firms in the tourism industry in the winter season of 2020/2021. Many blamed strict government regulations for this. However, government intervention also helped many firms to survive.
contexts.w23_21_3: Digital money, such as cryptocurrencies, is increasingly being used. Digital money transactions take place on electronic devices such as computers and smartphones. However, there can be market failure due to external costs arising from high energy usage of non-renewable sources. One way of reducing external costs is to tax the product.
contexts.w23_21_4: Malaysia once specialised in the production and export of natural rubber. The production of natural rubber was very labour-intensive. However, despite still being in the top 5 of natural rubber exporters in the world, Malaysia has moved towards producing manufactured goods that use natural rubber instead of just producing and exporting this primary product.
contexts.w23_21_5: One reason why the price of houses in cities such as Hong Kong, London, and New York is very high, is the low price elasticity of supply of houses. Trade unions in some of these cities are calling for more affordable housing for workers. Governments are also trying to implement various microeconomic policy measures to reduce the price of houses. In addition, the stability of the housing market can impact upon the effectiveness of monetary policy.

Source Material: Will Honduras become a more successful economy?

Honduras fact file 2020
• Population: 10m
• Population without access to electricity: 0.83m
• Unemployment rate: 6.1%
• Inflation rate: 4.2%
• Government budget deficit as % of GDP: 9.5%

Honduras is a lower middle-income country which relies heavily on trade with the US. More than half of Honduran exports go to the US and 40% of its imports come from the US. A high number of Hondurans work in the US and send money back home to their relatives.

Honduras used to concentrate on growing bananas and coffee, gaining skills and a good reputation in those industries. Now, Honduras produces a greater range of products including clothes, chemicals and paper. This diversification has reduced the uncertainty arising from sudden changes in demand and supply. For example, tariffs could be imposed on Honduran coffee or there could be a report stating that eating bananas is good for health.

While employment is declining in agriculture, it is increasing in the clothes industry in Honduras. Training for workers in the clothes industry is expected to increase and working conditions to improve. The firms are also using more capital goods. It is, however, uncertain what will happen to the prices of cotton, wool and other materials used to make clothes.

A successful clothes industry has the potential to reduce poverty in Honduras. The Honduran government tries to reduce poverty by, for example, providing unemployment benefit. A major reason for the government seeking to lower poverty is to increase life expectancy. Table 1.1 shows levels of poverty (percentage of population living on less than $1.90 a day) and life expectancy in selected countries.

Table 1.1: % of population living in poverty | Life expectancy (years)
• Chad: 38.1 | 54
• Honduras: 16.9 | 75
• Kenya: 37.1 | 66
• Maldives: 3.5 | 79
• South Sudan: 44.7 | 58
• Sweden: 0.2 | 83

A more successful Honduran economy would raise incomes. The country has a progressive income tax system, so there could be a significant rise in tax revenue. A more successful economy would also be likely to encourage more investment. Unemployment would be expected to fall which, in turn, could influence consumer spending.
contexts.w23_22_2: Botswana uses both capital goods and labour in its diamond mining industry. The country had an average economic growth rate of 3.8% between 2015 and 2019 compared to a global average of 2.8%. Over this period, the country experienced a low inflation rate and a move away from protectionism and towards free international trade.
contexts.w23_22_3: In 2020, some firms in Suriname, a South American country, stopped production. This was because the firms could not cover their variable costs, as well as some of their fixed costs. The reduction in the country's output resulted in a rise in its unemployment rate. The government used supply-side policy measures to reduce unemployment. In 2021, the number of firms in some markets fell again, but this time it was when output was rising.
contexts.w23_22_4: In the US, the supply of meat from emus, a large bird, is price-elastic. Recently, US farmers have switched to keeping other livestock and growing crops that changed their demand for labour. US farmers are influenced by the subsidies the government provides for the production of selected food items. Some people are reluctant to become farm workers as they think living standards are low in rural areas.
contexts.w23_22_5: In 2020, Singapore experienced a decrease in both its population size and its labour force. 2020 was a year of great change in a number of Singaporean markets. Some moved from disequilibrium to equilibrium. Despite all these changes, Singapore managed to increase its exports of goods and services.

Source Material: The challenges facing the Tunisian government

Tunisia fact file 2020
• Trade in goods and services balance: –$3bn
• Primary and secondary income balance: $0.6bn
• Unemployment rate: 17%
• Tunisian dinar (TND) / US dollar exchange rate: 1 TND = $0.35

Tunisia had a government budget deficit for a number of years. Between 2015 and 2020, the Tunisian government carried out reforms to reduce the tax burden, to rely more on indirect taxes and to make the tax system more efficient and more economical.

As well as taxing a range of products, the Tunisian government also regulates the price of some products including flour and milk. Government control of the price of flour and milk can help reduce poverty and prevent monopoly firms exploiting their market power. The Tunisian government also subsidises the production of electricity. The subsidy affects the cost of producing electricity, and the change in the price of electricity affects other firms' costs. This form of government spending can help reduce inflationary pressure but can also affect the efficiency of electricity production.

While some firms benefit from the subsidy on electricity production, they also experience periods when their other costs of production rise. Tunisian shoe producers have recently experienced a rise in wage costs and a decline in the number of workers they employ. (Fig. 1.1 in the original paper shows the change in average wage and the inflation rate in Tunisia, 2014–2020.)

Unemployment has been a problem in Tunisia for many years. In 2020, the government passed a law which promised that workers who had been unemployed for ten years or more would be employed by the public sector. To reduce the time spent moving between jobs, it increased labour market information available to workers and employers and did not raise unemployment benefit in line with inflation.

The Tunisian foreign exchange rate fluctuated in 2020. This affected the price of the country's exports and imports. It also affected the current account of its balance of payments, economic growth, inflation and unemployment.
contexts.s24_22_2: In 2020, wages paid to Mexican workers, including those in the primary sector, fell. This fall contributed to a 9% rise in poverty in the country. In the same year, many small and medium-sized firms closed down. The country also suffered from traffic congestion. Its capital, Mexico City, is the world's most congested city.
contexts.s24_22_3: South America is a large geographical area with millions of microeconomic decision-makers. During a recent pandemic, schools stayed closed for longer than anywhere else in the world. As a result, students received less education. The World Bank estimated that the average student would earn $24,000 less over their lifetime. Some students may earn only the minimum wage. In 2020, South America had an inflation rate of 6.3% and an economic growth rate of only 1.8%.
contexts.s24_22_4: Tajikistan is one of Asia's low-income countries. Its currency, the somoni, has the key characteristics of money. More than one million Tajik people work abroad, mostly in Russia. In 2020, the Tajik government was concerned that the country's economy might experience a recession which could cause a fall in tax revenue. Despite this possibility, some Tajik firms bought new capital equipment.
contexts.s24_22_5: Free goods and economic goods are consumed in Poland. In 2020, demand for both economic goods and factors of production increased in Poland. For example, Polish consumers demanded more football shirts and the Polish government increased its spending on housing for the country's population.

Source Material: Changes in Jordan's economy and population

Jordan fact file 2020
• Population: 11m
• Economic growth rate: –1.5%
• Labour force employed in the primary sector: 2%
• Labour force employed in the tertiary sector: 79%
• Unemployment rate: 23%
• Inflation rate: 2%
• Trade in services balance: –$1bn
• Import tariff revenue: $0.7bn
• Primary income balance: $0.8bn

In 2020, Jordan had a deficit on the current account of its balance of payments. This deficit contributed to a decline in Jordan's total demand in that year. This lower total demand was the most important reason why the number of workers was greater than the number of jobs available. Employment fell in most of Jordan's industries.

One of Jordan's main industries is tourism. Recent years have seen mergers between some of Jordan's tourism firms. These mergers reduced the prices of some holidays and raised their quality.

Jordan's population continues to grow. This is mainly because of net immigration, but also because the country's birth rate exceeds its death rate.

Changes in the size of a country's population affect the market for a range of products including clothing. An increase in population size also puts pressure on the country's sources of energy. The Jordanian government has several large renewable energy projects, and plans to spend even more on such projects. Greater reliance on renewable energy, including wind and solar power, can reduce environmental damage and can be relatively cheap in the long run. However, most renewable energy generators, including hydroelectric power stations, are expensive to build. Also, wind turbines and solar panels rely on favourable weather conditions.

Some of the spending by the Jordanian government is financed by borrowing. At the start of 2021, the Jordanian central bank was expected to raise the rate of interest. This was because total demand was predicted to increase and there would be a return to positive economic growth. A higher interest rate might affect Jordan's foreign exchange rate and investment.
contexts.w24_22_2: In 2021, the production point on the UK's production possibility curve (PPC) changed. Average wages increased. The average annual wage of a waiter was $23,580 while that of a chief executive of a large commercial bank was $1,617,000. A rise in wages enables people to eat in restaurants more often. Some of the food sold in UK restaurants is imported. In 2021, the UK government signed free trade agreements, removing import restrictions, with a number of countries.
contexts.w24_22_3: The central bank of Madagascar intervenes in the country's foreign exchange market. However, Madagascar has a largely market economic system. Nearly 70% of Madagascar's population live in poverty. Most of the country's industries are labour-intensive. In 2020, Madagascar had an economic growth rate of 6% and a deficit on the current account of its balance of payments of $0.6bn.
contexts.w24_22_4: In 2021, there were extensions and contractions in demand for a number of South African products. In that year, a South African court stopped a multinational company (MNC) exploring for oil along South Africa's coastline. South Africa experienced an increase in output, driven largely by the growth in its tertiary sector. However, its unemployment rate was 35%, a long way from full employment.
contexts.w24_22_5: The Peruvian government is under pressure from its industries to improve the country's transport system. Peru's third largest industry is tourism. There are many firms in the Peruvian tourism industry. Another major industry in Peru is fruit farming. In recent years, trade union membership in the Peruvian fruit-farming industry has increased.

Source Material: The future of the economy of St. Kitts and Nevis

St. Kitts and Nevis fact file 2022
• Population: 54,800
• GDP per head: $27,000
• Government spending: $310m
• Tax revenue: $292m
• Unemployment rate: 5.1%
• Inflation rate: 2.4%
• Current account balance of the balance of payments: –$56m

St. Kitts and Nevis is a small, two-island country in the Caribbean. The country's three main industries are tourism, financial services and agriculture. Tourists are attracted by the country's beaches, coral reefs, forts, rainforests and shipwrecks. However, if rainforests continue to be cut down and soil erosion continues to pollute the coral reefs, killing off marine life, tourism may be discouraged. The St. Kitts and Nevis Government is also concerned that the social costs of tourism exceed the private costs.

St. Kitts and Nevis's financial services include a growing banking sector. Among the country's commercial banks are a few foreign multinational companies (MNCs). These MNCs are attracted by the country's relatively high incomes, the absence of personal income tax and a relatively high literacy rate.

Some of the country's main agricultural products are carrots, onions, peanuts and sweet potatoes. In 2017, the St. Kitts and Nevis Government introduced a training scheme to raise the productivity of onion farmers.

Other important industries in St Kitts and Nevis include healthcare and fishing. Table 1.1 shows healthcare spending as a percentage of GDP and life expectancy in six selected countries in 2022.

Table 1.1: Healthcare spending as a % of GDP | Life expectancy (years), 2022
• Canada: 12.9 | 84
• Egypt: 4.5 | 75
• Haiti: 3.3 | 65
• Monaco: 1.9 | 90
• St. Kitts and Nevis: 5.4 | 77
• Sweden: 11.5 | 83

The small size of St. Kitts and Nevis's fishing industry means that it imports large quantities of fish. The country's fishing boats are small and some lack up-to-date equipment. A larger fishing industry, with bigger boats, may bring a number of benefits to the country.

Changes in the structure and performance of industries in St. Kitts and Nevis may alter the country's price level. Between 2018 and 2020, the country experienced deflation. This affected people's purchasing power, saving and debts. It also affected the country's exports and firms' investment decisions.
contexts.s25_22_2: The world's four largest accountancy firms experienced a decline in demand for their services at the start of 2023. One cause of this lower demand was a decline in mergers in other industries, including the chocolate industry. Three of the accountancy firms reduced the number of new workers they hired and the other accountancy firm announced job losses. The ability of workers to gain new jobs is influenced by their mobility.
contexts.s25_22_3: In 2022, Paraguay's production possibility curve (PPC) shifted to the right. Paraguay has a mixed economic system. Its government provides merit goods and public goods. The country's private sector is a major producer of shampoo. The firms in the shampoo industry make use of division of labour. There are several firms in the industry, but the number is declining. There is a possibility that soon there may be just one firm in the industry.
contexts.s25_22_4: In 2022, more than a quarter of a million workers, including doctors, left Sri Lanka to work in other countries. This was largely due to economic problems, including an inflation rate of 50% and a concern that unemployment might rise. The Sri Lankan Government increased direct taxation. It also encouraged some public sector workers to work abroad temporarily. People who work abroad often send money home to relatives.
contexts.s25_22_5: In 2023, the Chinese Government said that it would aim for an economic growth rate of 5% and a steady increase in both exports and imports. It was expected that higher output would be caused mainly by an increase in household spending, although this could also result in inflation. Another aim of the Chinese Government was to keep the unemployment rate at around 5.5%. China has an ageing population and an ageing labour force.

Source Material: Is there a future for Australian coal?

(Australia fact file | 2021 | 2026 (forecast))
Population | 25.8m | 27.1m
Labour force | 14.0m | 14.8m
Number unemployed | 0.56m | 0.62m
GDP | $1618bn | $2017bn
Government budget balance | –3.2% of GDP | –

Australia is a major producer of coal. Most coal is used to produce electricity. In this process, carbon dioxide is emitted. Global demand for coal has declined in recent years as countries have tried to reduce pollution. There has been a switch to, for example, gas, offshore wind and solar power.

Coal is mined in each of Australia's six states but most is mined in Queensland and in New South Wales. In Queensland, some of the firms are very large. These firms employ both low-paid, unskilled workers and high-paid, specialist mining engineers, site managers and accountants. The firms use the latest excavators, mining drills, crushing equipment, earth movers and drones to detect maintenance issues.

Coal can be stored to meet changes in market conditions but storage costs can be high. It can also take years to construct a new coal mine. Table 1.1 shows the output and consumption of the seven largest producers in 2020.

Table 1.1: Output of coal (million tonnes) | Consumption of coal (million tonnes)
• China: 3640 | 4215
• India: 765 | 939
• US: 671 | 660
• Australia: 515 | 121
• Indonesia: 510 | 142
• Russia: 419 | 234
• South Africa: 250 | 186

Global coal production has fallen in recent years with most countries switching to renewable sources of energy. However, there are some countries where coal production is set to increase. There are plans in both Australia and India, for example, to open new coal mines. The Indonesian government sets a maximum price on coal to encourage the country's power stations to use it.

The Australian coal industry contributes to its government's tax revenue. There are, however, other influences on Australia's government's budget balance including changes in tax rates and state support for some of the country's industries.
contexts.s23_21_2: Living standards, including education, have improved for most people in South Africa in recent years. Most households have more money and the government has more tax revenue. There is, however, considerable income inequality. In 2020, 36% of the population were living in poverty. An increase in unemployment benefit payments might reduce this poverty.
contexts.s23_21_3: Germany's death rate is higher than some other countries, including Sweden, Cuba and the Maldives. Germany's labour force increased in size between 2011 and 2021 and has become even more productive. The country has also experienced low inflation and a growing surplus on the current account of its balance of payments.
contexts.s23_21_4: Many people from the Philippines work in another country, often in industries that provide merit goods and public goods. In 2020, the Philippine government raised more tax revenue. Some was spent on policy measures to increase life expectancy and some on policy measures to reduce unemployment. The country's unemployment rate was also affected by a rise in the country's foreign exchange rate.
contexts.s23_21_5: In Greece, rich households spend more than the average household. The amount of spending in an economy influences whether its production point is on or inside its production possibility curve (PPC). In 2020, household spending in Greece fell. This affected some firms' plans to merge. It also increased unemployment. More than half of those unemployed in Greece had been unemployed for more than a year.

Source Material: How will oil change Guyana?

Guyana fact file 2020
• Population: 790 000
• Estimated optimum population: 1 100 000
• Proportion of population living in poverty: 35%
• Economic growth rate: 26%
• Unemployment rate: 11%
• Current account of the balance of payments: –$237m

Guyana was the fastest growing economy in the world in 2020. Sugar, gold and timber have accounted for a relatively high proportion of the country's output and exports for some time. In 2020, the sugar industry was hit by bad weather and falling global demand. In contrast, the output of gold and timber increased.

The main reason why Guyana's real GDP increased so rapidly was the increase in oil production. Oil was discovered offshore by a foreign multinational company (MNC) in 2015 and the MNC started production in 2019. It is predicted that Guyana will become the world's largest oil producer per head by 2025.

The Guyanese government is planning to use some of the tax revenue it will raise from oil to spend on education and improvements to the country's infrastructure. Planned projects include new railway lines and stations. A more extensive and cheaper rail service may enable more people to work further from home and may influence the market for substitutes, such as car transport. The Guyanese government is also planning to spend some of the tax revenue on improving the country's access to the internet. Table 1.1 shows GDP per head and internet access in seven countries in 2020.

Table 1.1: GDP per head ($) | Population with internet access (%)
• Brazil: 8717 | 72
• Eritrea: 643 | 2
• France: 40 494 | 83
• Guyana: 6160 | 39
• Iceland: 66 945 | 99
• Morocco: 3204 | 64
• Zambia: 1305 | 29

Guyana has experienced a slow growth in its population size in recent years. In 2020, its birth rate was 16.5, its death rate was 6.8 and its net migration rate was –7.7. With increases in oil production, emigration may decline and the country may start to experience net immigration. A higher population may affect Guyana in a number of ways including changing the size of its labour force and affecting the environment.
contexts.s23_22_2: In 2020, the largest Thai commercial bank merged with a smaller commercial Thai bank. It was expected that the merger would affect the price charged for bank services and the amount that would be lent. Thai commercial banks operate in the private sector. A growing private sector can move an economy towards a market economic system.
contexts.s23_22_3: Canada's private sector firms have a number of different objectives. The quantity and quality of land used by these firms, including farms, has increased. There has also been increased investment with the firms buying more capital goods. In 2021, the Canadian government encouraged higher investment and aimed to prevent a rise in unemployment.
contexts.s23_22_4: In 2020, Australia had a high national minimum wage (NMW). The NMW is received by some people who work on Australian dairy farms. Australia produces milk and soft drinks. Milk is purchased by some people as an alternative to soft drinks. Some dairy farms and some small firms went out of business in 2020. The year saw an increase in the value of the country's floating foreign exchange rate.
contexts.s23_22_5: In 2019, China's economic growth rate was 6.1% and Chinese households increased their spending. More Chinese people attended sports events and the earnings of top sportspeople increased. China exported more despite a rise in tariffs on some of its products. For example, the US imposed higher tariffs on the imports of Chinese tea and coffee.

Source Material: New Zealand's aim for carbon-neutrality

New Zealand fact file 2020
• Total GDP: $195bn
• Total GDP as a percentage of world GDP: 0.16%
• Population: 5m

New Zealand is a relatively small economy that intends to be carbon-neutral by the year 2050. Carbon-neutrality is when a country removes the same amount of carbon dioxide from the environment as it emits or simply eliminating carbon dioxide emissions altogether.

There are now various plans in place to reduce external costs in industries such as the milk and car industries. Both industries are major contributors to air pollution and the milk industry damages the environment where many wild animals live. The government intends to end imports of petrol-powered cars by 2032 and also limit the number of cows that each farmer can keep. However, good substitutes will need to be found to achieve these targets. Consumers will want a cheaper substitute for petrol-powered cars and farmers will need a different source of revenue than cows.

The success of the government plans will be important for New Zealand's macroeconomic performance. New Zealand exporters rely on a clean and green brand image, and this will help economic growth and reduce the deficit on the current account of the balance of payments. However, not all firms will benefit from government plans to achieve carbon-neutrality and inflation rates may also increase.

A switch to a carbon-neutral economy could result in increased unemployment due to significant job losses in the coal, oil and gas industries. This could lead to increased poverty in certain communities and large losses in the firms that serve these communities. However, these changes may be temporary and an economy with a high mobility of factors of production could avoid such problems.

The good news is that New Zealand already has a low level of carbon dioxide emissions. However, not all countries can easily take the route New Zealand is planning to take. For selected countries, Table 1.1 shows their share of world GDP (%) and their share of world carbon dioxide emissions (%) in 2018.

Table 1.1: Share of world GDP (%) | Share of world carbon dioxide emissions (%)
• China: 16.1 | 29.7
• Japan: 5.7 | 3.2
• New Zealand: 0.2 | 0.1
• Thailand: 0.6 | 0.7
• United Kingdom: 3.3 | 1.0
• United States: 23.8 | 13.9
contexts.s23_23_2: Liechtenstein is a high-income economy in the middle of Europe. The country's low tax rates and low levels of regulation make it an attractive place for foreign firms and individuals to open bank accounts. Firms' costs of production in Liechtenstein are high but this is slightly offset by low indirect taxation.
contexts.s23_23_3: The number of Chinese restaurants in the UK fell by approximately 7% in 2020 compared to the year before. Reasons for this include falling demand for Chinese food and increasing competition from other types of food. Some small firms selling Chinese food are also unwilling to invest in the latest technology because of the possible opportunity costs.
contexts.s23_23_4: After the recession that struck Albania in 2013, the country experienced a significant rise in emigration. Albanian workers and students in other countries have expressed little desire to return. However, the government is trying to implement policy measures that could attract more people to return to the country.
contexts.s23_23_5: The food processing, tourism, and education industries all contribute significantly to the government budget for the US state of Wisconsin. The contribution of the education industry is higher than that of other industries due to the higher wages earned in education. This industry also contributes to the population growth of the state. This not only creates private benefits but also external benefits.

Source Material: Changes in the economy of Montenegro

Montenegro fact file 2020
• Population: 608 000
• GDP: $4.8bn
• Government budget deficit: –$0.6bn
• Unemployment rate: 18.0%
• Inflation rate: 0.4%

Montenegro is a European country that has seen an increase in the role of its private sector. By 2020, 90% of state-owned firms had been privatised. All commercial banking, telecommunications and aluminium production has been transferred to the private sector. The country's banks now have more computers, more workers and more office buildings.

Most years, Montenegro attracts three times as many tourists as the number of people who live in the country. Tourism is a very competitive market. Demand for holidays is price-elastic which has implications for the pricing strategy of firms in the industry. The proportion of workers employed in tourism and other tertiary sector industries has increased. In 2020, 75% of Montenegro's labour force were employed in the tertiary sector.

Some of the workers employed in the primary sector help in the growth and export of oranges. It has been suggested that a minimum price should be set for oranges and some other crops. Changes in the price of a country's exports can affect both the trade in goods and services balance and the current account balance of its balance of payments. Table 1.1 gives selected details of six East European countries' balance of payments in 2020.

Table 1.1: Trade in goods and services balance ($ million) | Current account balance ($ million)
• Bosnia & Herzegovina: –2914 | –624
• Bulgaria: 2318 | 2742
• Croatia: –317 | 1456
• Kosovo: –2141 | –459
• Montenegro: –1174 | –837
• Slovenia: 4609 | 3049

A country's international trade position is influenced by the amount and pattern of consumer spending. Privatisation has had an influence on consumer spending. Moving to the private sector has affected investment, the number of workers employed and competition in those industries. It has also affected firms' objectives, prices and their responsiveness to changes in consumer demand. In 2020, Montenegro experienced very low inflation. It was expected that this could turn into deflation. A fall in the price level could affect the country's output, employment and balance of payments.
contexts.w23_23_2: In 2019, Mozambique was hit by a serious storm which destroyed bridges, factories, roads and electricity lines. Almost 60% of Mozambique's population live in absolute poverty. The country's people are keen to increase Mozambique's economic development. There is a high level of government intervention in Mozambique's economy. Although Mozambique does not impose import quotas, it does impose a range of import tariffs.
contexts.w23_23_3: Saudi Arabia's economic system may change in the future. The country's central bank is dealing with more private sector banks. In 2020, the population's average age of 31.8 was just above the global average of 31.2. In that year, plans were announced to build a city where no cars would be needed or allowed. Such a development might encourage more young people to move to Saudi Arabia.
contexts.w23_23_4: People in Ecuador buy products using a variety of forms of money. The Ecuadorian government pays public sector workers' wages directly into their bank accounts. In 2019, some Ecuadorian firms' profits were affected by advances in technology. That year, the Ecuadorian government cut public sector workers' hours and, in 2020, it reduced its spending. Economists were uncertain what effect the decrease in government spending would have on unemployment.
contexts.w23_23_5: In 2020, Paraguay's Consumer Prices Index rose by 3% and its foreign exchange rate fluctuated. Each year Paraguay experiences net emigration. People leave a country for a number of reasons. These include a low rate of economic growth and high level of market failure. The Paraguayan government does intervene in the economy in an attempt to reduce market failure.

questions.text: Calculate St. Kitts and Nevis's government budget deficit in 2022.
Identify two examples of the factor of production 'land' in St. Kitts and Nevis.

questions.text: Explain how tourism causes external costs in St. Kitts and Nevis.
questions.ms: 1 mark for meaning: social costs exceed private costs / harmful effects on third parties not involved in producing or consuming (1). 1 mark for a tourism example from the country: pollution / environmental damage / death of wildlife or marine life / overcrowding (1).

questions.text: Explain two reasons why a foreign bank may open a branch in St. Kitts and Nevis.
questions.ms: 1 mark per reason + 1 per explanation. High incomes (1) high demand for banking services and loans / borrowers can repay / high profit (1). No personal income tax (1) people keep all their income, more disposable income (1). High literacy rate (1) aware of benefits of bank accounts / skilled, productive workers (1). Explanation marks depend on the reason.

questions.text: Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effect of an increase in the productivity of onion farmers on the market for onions.
questions.ms: 1 mark each: axes labelled price and quantity (1); original demand and supply curves labelled (1); SUPPLY curve shifts right (1); equilibria shown P1/Q1 and P2/Q2 or E1/E2 (1).

questions.text: Analyse the relationship between healthcare spending as a percentage of GDP and life expectancy.
questions.ms: Expected relationship: direct / positive (1) higher spending, higher life expectancy (1). Evidence (must compare): Haiti second lowest spending and shortest life expectancy (1); Canada and Sweden spend a high % and have long life expectancy (1). Analysis: more spending improves health / quality of care / preventative care, lowers death rate (1). Exception: Monaco (1) lowest % but longest life expectancy (1). Analysis of exception: 1.9% of a very high GDP can be more than 12.9% of a lower GDP (1); other influences e.g. nutrition, education, housing (1). Max 5.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not an increase in the size of its fishing industry would benefit St. Kitts and Nevis.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for might, up to 4 for might not, max 6.
Might: fewer fish imports (1) less risk of supply shocks (1) fish can be exported (1) better current account (1); more employment (1) higher incomes (1) living standards (1) GDP / growth (1) tax revenue (1); economies of scale (1) example (1) lower average cost (1) lower fish prices (1); bigger boats more productive (1) more profitable industry (1).
Might not: opportunity cost (1) resources could be used elsewhere (1); over-fishing (1) depletes fish stocks (1) higher prices long run (1); diseconomies of scale (1) higher average cost (1); external costs (1) damage to coral reefs / pollution (1) harms tourism (1); dangerous / low-paid / low-skilled work, seasonal unemployment (1); over-specialisation (1) exposed to falling fish demand or foreign competition (1).
questions.subtopic: 5.4 Differences in economic development between countries

questions.text: Discuss whether or not deflation is likely to have harmed St. Kitts and Nevis.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for harmed, up to 4 for not harmed, max 6.
Harmed: raises real value of debt (1) defaults (1) less investment (1); deflationary spiral (1) from lower total demand (1) lower output / recession (1) more unemployment (1) lower wages (1); lower confidence (1) discourages MNCs (1); people delay buying (1) waiting for lower prices (1).
Not harmed: higher purchasing power / real income (1) people may consume more (1); value of savings rises (1) more wealth (1); may come from higher total supply (1) new technology / lower costs (1) higher output (1) more employment (1); more internationally competitive, cheaper exports (1) more export revenue (1) fewer imports (1) better current account (1). 1 mark for malign vs benign deflation.

questions.text: Identify two advantages a firm may gain from merging with another firm.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: less competition / more market power or share; economies of scale / lower average cost; control over outlets; control over raw materials; rationalisation; more profit / revenue; new ideas / technology; spread risks; more resources; more sales; consumer data. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two disadvantages workers may experience as a result of losing their jobs.
questions.ms: 1 mark per disadvantage + 1 per explanation. Loss of income (1) lower living standards / can't afford necessities (1); loss of skills (1) harder to find another job (1); more likely to get into debt (1) harder to repay loans (1); harder to get a loan (1); loss of fringe benefits (1) e.g. health insurance (1); less attractive to employers (1); stress / mental health problems (1) loss of confidence (1); may sell possessions (1) to pay bills (1); demotivation (1) become a discouraged worker (1); less ability to save (1). 'Harder to get another job' rewarded once only.

questions.text: Analyse the advantages of an increase in labour mobility.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Workers can change jobs more easily (1) occupational mobility (1) improve skills / productivity (1). Can move area (1) geographical mobility (1). Reduces structural / regional / frictional (1) unemployment (1) workers find new jobs faster (1) higher paid jobs / living standards (1) more tax revenue, less spent on benefits (1). Fewer labour shortages (1) lower costs / less cost-push inflation (1) more output / growth (1). Firms respond faster to changes in consumer demand (1) fewer surpluses and shortages (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not the demand for chocolate is likely to be price elastic.
questions.ms:
Might: has substitutes; may be seen as a luxury; demand for particular brands is more elastic than for chocolate as a whole; the longer the time period, the easier it is to change spending patterns.
Might not: may be addictive; may be seen as a necessity; takes up a small % of income.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify what is measured on the axes of a production possibility curve.
questions.ms: (Output of) two types of product (2). Or: output (1) of one product (1) and another product (1). Max 2.

questions.text: Explain, with an example of each, the difference between a merit good and a public good.
questions.ms: Merit good: under-consumed / consumers don't appreciate its full value / external benefits / can be private sector / rival and excludable (1) e.g. education, healthcare (1). Public good: wouldn't be provided by the private sector / provided by government (1) non-excludable, non-rival (1) e.g. street lighting, defence, flood control (1). Max 2 each. No mark for roads unless qualified.

questions.text: Analyse how division of labour can benefit firms.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Workers specialise (1) in what they're best at (1) saves time (1) less waste (1) fewer mistakes (1) higher productivity / skill (1) more output (1) lower average cost (1). Higher quality (1) lower prices (1) more sales (1) more revenue (1) more profit (1). Easier to mechanise (1) less labour needed (1). Less training needed (1) as each worker does fewer tasks (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not consumers would benefit from only one firm producing shampoo.
questions.ms:
Might: economies of scale; lower average cost may mean lower prices; high profits and security may fund lots of R&D; quality may be high; less time choosing.
Might not: lack of competition may push up prices; less choice; if quality is poor there's no substitute to switch to; the firm may suffer diseconomies of scale.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two types of unemployment.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: frictional; structural; cyclical / demand-deficient. Also accept voluntary, involuntary, seasonal, classical, casual, regional, technological. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two ways that money received from relatives working abroad could raise their families' living standards.
questions.ms: 1 mark per way + 1 per explanation. Buy more products / necessities (1) less poverty (1); better quality food (1) better nutrition / health (1); spend on education (1) higher earning potential (1); healthcare (1) higher life expectancy (1); housing (1) less illness (1); luxuries (1) e.g. holiday / car (1); start a small business (1) earn income (1); pay off debts (1) less stress (1); save more (1) earn interest / pay future costs (1); work fewer hours (1). No marks for why the money might be large.

questions.text: Analyse how an increase in direct taxation could increase unemployment.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Higher income tax (1) or wealth tax (1) cuts disposable income (1) less consumer spending (1) lower total demand (1) lower demand for workers (1) since labour is a derived demand (1) more cyclical unemployment (1). Less incentive to work (1) benefits may pay more than a lower paid job (1) more voluntary / frictional unemployment (1). Higher corporation tax (1) cuts profit kept (1) firms cut output / less incentive to expand (1) less investment (1) cut jobs to protect profit (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a doctor would benefit from working in another country.
questions.ms:
Might: higher pay and living standards; lower inflation; lower taxes; more chance of a job or promotion; better working conditions; more fringe benefits; new skills and experience; safer environment; can send money home; better opportunities for their children.
Might not: longer hours; fewer holidays; less job security; misses friends and family; discrimination; language / cultural barriers. Max 4 if the answer discusses another city rather than another country.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two influences on household spending.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: income; interest rate; taxation; confidence; inflation / prices; wealth; age; household size; culture; advertising; quality; tastes. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two advantages of employing older workers.
questions.ms: 1 mark per advantage + 1 per explanation. More experienced (1) higher productivity / skills (1); fewer mistakes (1) higher quality (1); reliable (1) punctual / careful (1); need little training (1) keeps costs low (1); less likely to take parental leave (1) less disruption (1); can train younger workers (1); less likely to leave (1); keeps older people healthy (1); raises incomes of older people (1) less poverty (1); larger labour force (1); may accept fewer hours (1) more flexibility (1); relate better to older customers (1) a growing market (1).

questions.text: Analyse how an increase in household spending could cause inflation.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Household spending (consumption) is a component of total demand (1) so total demand rises (1). Total demand may exceed total supply (1) firms raise prices (1) demand-pull inflation (1). Firms may invest (1) and raise output (1) hiring more workers (1) pushing up wages (1) and demand for raw materials (1) raising their prices (1) raising costs of production (1) cost-push inflation (1) wage-price spiral (1). AD = C + I + G + (X – M) accepted.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a government should aim for an increase in imports.
questions.ms:
Should: saves scarce resources; reduces shortages at home; more choice and quality; imports technology; cheaper raw materials and capital goods cut firms' costs; more competition makes domestic firms efficient; more tariff revenue; can consume more than it produces short term; raises incomes abroad, boosting demand for its exports.
Should not: worsens the current account; some domestic firms may close; may reduce the exchange rate; less employment; lower incomes / GDP per head; lower long-term living standards; don't want to import demerit goods.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Explain the main type of unemployment experienced by Jordan in 2020.
questions.ms: Cyclical / demand-deficient unemployment (1) caused by lower total demand / employment fell in most industries / more workers than jobs available (1). 'Fall in demand' alone is not enough, it must be total (macro) demand.

questions.text: Explain two advantages the Jordanian economy may gain from the mergers between its tourism firms.
questions.ms: 1 mark per advantage + 1 per explanation. Lower prices (1) may raise output / GDP / employment / living standards, may come from economies of scale (1). Higher quality (1) may raise exports / tourism revenue / foreign currency, reduce current account deficit, more internationally competitive, may come from sharing ideas (1).

questions.text: Analyse, using a demand and supply diagram, how an increase in population size will affect the market for clothing.
questions.ms: Diagram (up to 4): axes labelled price and quantity (1); original demand and supply curves labelled (1); DEMAND curve shifts right (1); equilibria shown P1/Q1 and P2/Q2 or E1/E2 (1). Written (1): larger population means more consumers, higher demand for clothes, price rises (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not the Jordanian government should spend more on renewable energy.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for should, up to 4 for should not, max 6.
Should: more energy needed as population grows (1) non-renewables will run out / less reliance on fossil fuels (1) lower import bills (1); less environmental damage (1) fewer external costs / less pollution (1) less climate change, sustainable development (1) better health (1); cheaper in the long run (1) sun and wind are free goods (1) lower production costs (1) lower household bills (1).
Should not: expensive to build (1) opportunity cost (1) with example (1); relies on weather (1) so supply may be unreliable (1); higher cost if interest rates are high (1) may be funded by borrowing (1) or higher taxes (1); visual pollution (1) e.g. wind turbines (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not the Jordanian central bank should have raised the rate of interest in 2021.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for should have, up to 4 for should not, max 6.
Should: total demand predicted to rise, so a higher rate reduces it (1) encourages saving (1) discourages spending / borrowing (1) lowers demand-pull (1) inflation (1) reduces imports (1); attracts more funds the government can borrow (1) e.g. for renewable energy (1).
Should not: raises the cost of government borrowing / harder to repay debt (1); discourages investment (1) lower growth (1) less employment growth / unemployment (1); may raise the exchange rate (1) via hot money inflows (1) higher export prices, cheaper imports, fewer exports, more imports (1) less tourism (1) bigger current account deficit (1).

questions.text: Identify two places where a production point could be located on a PPC diagram.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: inside / below the curve; on the curve; outside / above the curve. May be shown on a diagram.

questions.text: Explain two reasons why someone may switch from eating in one restaurant to eating in another restaurant.
questions.ms: 1 mark per reason + 1 per explanation. Price (1) lower price more affordable / substitutes (1); quality (1) better ingredients, service, taste, new menu (1); convenience (1) longer opening hours / better location (1); facilities (1); income (1) can afford more expensive restaurants (1); tastes (1) e.g. switch to a vegan restaurant (1); advertising (1) persuades customers (1); portion size (1) value for money (1).

questions.text: Analyse why the wage of a chief executive of a large commercial bank is higher than that of a waiter.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Chief executive more qualified / educated (1) more training (1) more skilled (1) more productive (1) more experienced (1) more responsibility / stress (1) in shorter supply / harder to replace (1) more inelastic supply (1). Higher demand (1) more inelastic demand (1). Stronger bargaining power (1) e.g. professional body (1). Less likely to face discrimination (1) e.g. migrant workers (1). Longer hours (1). No marks for 'banks are more profitable than restaurants'.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not free trade will increase economic growth.
questions.ms:
Might: countries specialise in what they're best at; more competition raises productivity and cuts costs, boosting demand; cheaper raw materials and capital goods; access to larger markets lets firms expand output.
Might not: infant industries can't grow; declining industries close faster; imports replace domestic output; less tax (tariff) revenue; firms may gain monopoly power and restrict output; unfair competition e.g. dumping.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Define foreign exchange market.
questions.ms: An arrangement / place (1) where different countries' currencies are bought (1) and sold (1) / one currency is exchanged for another (1). Max 2.

questions.text: Explain two reasons why a firm may adopt labour-intensive production.
questions.ms: 1 mark per reason + 1 per explanation. Labour is cheap / low wages (1) cheaper than capital / high supply of labour (1); labour very productive (1) low costs of production (1); government subsidises employment (1) to cut unemployment (1); personal services (1) individual attention (1); labour is creative / adaptable (1) high quality / better methods (1); labour is unskilled (1) can't use high-tech capital (1).

questions.text: Analyse how the macroeconomic aims of economic growth and balance of payments stability may conflict.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Growth raises employment (1) and incomes (1) so imports rise (1). Higher consumer spending (1) firms switch to the domestic market (1) fewer exports (1) current account deficit (1). Firms import more raw materials (1) and capital goods (1). Growth may cause inflation (1) making domestic products less price competitive (1). Growth may deplete resources (1) increasing need for imports (1). Export-led growth may raise the exchange rate (1) raising imports / cutting exports (1). Growth may be export-led / from restricting imports (1) causing a surplus (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a high level of poverty is likely to exist in a market economic system.
questions.ms:
Might: unemployment; lack of welfare benefits; income inequality; merit goods like healthcare and education under-consumed and under-produced; monopolies may develop and raise prices.
Might not: competition and profit motive keep prices low; efficiency encouraged, bringing high wages and employment; quick response to consumer demand may raise growth; efficient private firms may leave relative poverty but little absolute poverty.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Define an extension in demand.
questions.ms: A movement along a demand curve (1) with higher quantity demanded (1) caused by a fall (1) in price (1). Max 2. Not 'an increase in demand', but accept 'an increase in quantity demanded'.

questions.text: Explain two external costs that may be caused by exploring for oil.
questions.ms: 1 mark per cost + 1 per explanation. Air pollution (1) worse air quality / health / climate change (1); noise pollution (1) disturbs sleep (1); water pollution / oil spills (1) damage health (1); damage to the natural environment / land (1) destroys wildlife habitats (1); less tourism (1) lower employment (1); congestion (1) higher transport costs (1).

questions.text: Analyse how growth in a country's tertiary sector can increase its living standards.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. High productivity (1) more output (1) more employment (1). Higher wages (1) so workers can buy more goods, education, healthcare, less poverty (1). Better working conditions (1) less physically demanding (1) better health (1) fewer accidents (1). More education (1) future skills (1) earnings (1) quality of output (1) higher HDI (1). More transport services (1) less congestion (1). Entertainment industry (1) better leisure (1). More healthcare (1) higher life expectancy (1). More tax revenue (1) to spend on e.g. education (1). Less pollution (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not workers who lose their jobs are likely to stay unemployed for a long time.
questions.ms:
Might: lose skills, and unskilled workers find it harder to get work; become out of date with technology; costly to retrain; lose confidence; less attractive to employers; more likely if cyclical / structural rather than frictional; high unemployment benefits.
Might not: government training; geographically / occupationally mobile; gap between wages and benefits encourages job search; growing economy creates jobs; may leave the labour force e.g. retire / emigrate; may be seasonally unemployed.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two examples of labour employed in the tourism industry.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2, e.g. tour guide; hotel manager / worker; travel agent; flight attendant; coach / bus driver. Also accept skilled and unskilled. Not 'driver' on its own.

questions.text: Explain two reasons why countries with a good transport system often have a high GDP.
questions.ms: 1 mark per reason + 1 per explanation. Lower firms' costs (1) cheaper / more efficient to move goods, more competitive, more exports, bigger markets (1); less wastage (1) food arrives fresh, higher profits (1); more labour mobility (1) less unemployment / higher productivity (1); less congestion (1) less time lost (1); more tourism earnings (1); attracts MNCs / FDI (1) more employment / productive capacity (1); fewer accidents (1) fewer lost working hours (1); less pollution (1) healthier workforce (1).

questions.text: Analyse the benefits consumers may gain from a competitive market.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Many firms / no barriers to entry (1) substitutes available (1). Low prices (1) as firms compete for market share / consumers (1). High quality (1) as competition raises efficiency (1) and innovation (1). More choice / variety (1). Responsive to changes in consumer demand (1) consumer sovereignty (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not an increase in trade union membership will benefit an economy.
questions.ms:
Might: higher wages and better conditions may raise productivity; higher wages raise total demand and real GDP; better conditions raise living standards; channel of communication reduces conflict between workers and employers; help with training may raise output.
Might not: higher wages may cause inflation; industrial action e.g. strikes lowers output / GDP; may resist job losses / new technology, blocking efficiency gains. Max L2 (4) if the answer misreads the question as higher union fees.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

options: any policy designed to decrease inflation
any policy designed to decrease unemployment

The surplus produce is sold to the government.

questions.text:

options: the cost of updating existing price lists
the real income of fixed-income earners
the real value of consumer debt

a lack of internal diseconomies of scale

(change in GDP (%) | inflation rate (%))
questions.ms: Answer: B (10 | 7)

questions.text: Which type of unemployment is generally regarded by economists as the least serious for the economy?
questions.ms: Answer: B (frictional)

questions.text:
The Consumer Prices Index (CPI) for a country rose during one year from 125 to 150.
What was the country's rate of inflation?
questions.ms: Answer: A (20%)

questions.text: What does the Human Development Index (HDI) indicate?
questions.ms: Answer: C (living standards)

questions.text: What best describes relative poverty?
options: A 12-year-old boy has never been able to access a doctor or school.
A person earns less than the minimum defined level of income.
A person has a lower living standard than the minimum level acceptable in a society.
A person is unable to afford the basic necessities of life.
questions.ms: Answer: C (A person has a lower living standard than the minimum level acceptable in a society.)

questions.text:
The table shows population statistics for three countries in a particular year.
What can be concluded from the table?
options: country X has fewer females than country Y
country Y has the smallest population increase
country Y has the highest living standards
country Z has a decreasing population
questions.ms: Answer: D (country Z has a decreasing population)

questions.text: What is most likely to promote international specialisation?
options: similarities in climate in different countries
similarities in the availability of natural resources in different countries
the abolition of tariffs and customs duties
questions.ms: Answer: D (the abolition of tariffs and customs duties)

questions.text:
What are the effects on price and equilibrium quantity of the imposition of an import tariff on a good?
(price | equilibrium quantity)
questions.ms: Answer: C (increases | decreases)

questions.text:
The diagram shows the market for the Indian rupee in US$.
What will cause the demand curve for rupees to shift from D1 to D2?
options: a fall in Indian exports to the US
a fall in the US inflation rate
a rise in foreign direct investment into India
a rise in interest rates in the US
questions.ms: Answer: C (a rise in foreign direct investment into India)

questions.text:
The diagram shows China’s trade with Brazil for two years.
What happened to China’s trade balance with Brazil between year 1 and year 2?
options: It moved from deficit to surplus.
It moved from surplus to deficit.
questions.ms: Answer: D (It moved from surplus to deficit.)
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text: Calculate Tunisia's balance on the current account of its balance of payments.
questions.ms: 1 mark: –$2.4bn (–$3bn + $0.6bn). Also accept –6.8 or –6.9 billion TND.
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text: Identify two qualities of a good tax that the Tunisian government aimed to achieve.
questions.ms: 1 mark each: efficient (improves market performance / reduces market failure); economical (raises more in revenue than it costs to collect). Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain one reason why the Tunisian government regulates the price of flour and milk.
questions.ms: 1 mark reason + 1 mark explanation. Reduce poverty (1) flour and milk are basic necessities, keeps them affordable / price low (1). OR prevent monopoly firms exploiting market power (1) stops firms raising price to a high level (1).

questions.text: Explain two ways the Tunisian government tried to reduce frictional unemployment.
questions.ms: 1 mark per way + 1 per explanation. Increased labour market information for workers and employers (1) so workers know about vacancies / skills needed, reducing search time and moving between jobs faster (1). Did not raise unemployment benefit in line with inflation (1) so its purchasing power falls, increasing the incentive to work (1).

questions.text: Analyse, using a demand and supply diagram, how an increase in wage costs would affect the market for shoes.
questions.ms: Diagram (up to 4): axes labelled price and quantity (1); original demand and supply curves labelled (1); supply curve shifts LEFT (1); equilibria shown P1/Q1 and P2/Q2 or E1/E2 (1). Written (1): higher wage costs raise costs of production, which raises price (1). Higher price must be linked to higher costs.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not the Tunisian government should continue to subsidise electricity production.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for why it should, up to 4 for why not, max 6.
Should: lowers cost of producing electricity (1) raises supply (1) lowers price (1) more affordable / less poverty (1); lowers costs of firms using electricity (1) so they expand / attract MNCs / more output and growth (1) more employment (1); reduces inflation (1) more internationally competitive, more exports, better current account (1); less pollution if subsidising green energy (1).
Should not: electricity firms may rely on the subsidy (1) become inefficient (1) may not pass on lower prices (1); opportunity cost (1) money could go on e.g. healthcare (1); budget deficit / higher taxes (1); pollution if e.g. coal powered / depletes non-renewables (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a rise in the value of the Tunisian dinar would benefit the Tunisian economy.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for might benefit, up to 4 for might not, max 6.
Might: cheaper imports (1) reduce inflation (1) households can buy more imports / more choice (1) cheaper raw materials / capital goods (1) lower costs of production (1) more competitive pressure on domestic firms (1); lower total demand reduces demand-pull inflation (1); sign of a strong economy / confidence (1) attracts investment / MNCs (1); if export demand is price inelastic, export revenue may rise (1).
Might not: higher export prices (1) fewer exports / less export revenue (1) cheaper imports so more imports (1) less international competitiveness (1) bigger current account deficit (1); lower net exports reduce GDP / growth (1) raise unemployment (1); may discourage MNCs (1) higher cost of setting up (1). Lower total demand can be credited once only.

questions.text: Identify two possible opportunity costs of producing primary sector products.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: secondary sector / manufactured / capital goods; tertiary sector products / services; wildlife habitats / quality of the ecosystem. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two policy measures which may reduce poverty.
questions.ms: 1 mark per measure + 1 per explanation. E.g. introduce / raise minimum wage (1) raises income of low-paid (1); state benefits (1) e.g. unemployment benefit lets people buy necessities (1); cut indirect taxes (1) these fall more heavily on the poor (1); education / training (1) raises earning potential (1); job creation / public sector jobs (1) raise incomes (1); subsidies (1) lower prices (1); lower interest rates (1) firms expand and hire (1); more government spending (1) more jobs (1); cut direct taxes (1) more disposable income (1); progressive taxes (1) cut relative poverty (1); job information (1) less frictional unemployment (1); maximum prices (1) necessities more affordable (1).

questions.text: Analyse how the closure of firms may harm consumers.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Less competition (1) more monopoly power (1) higher prices (1) less innovation / R&D, complacency (1) lower quality (1) slower to respond to consumer demand (1). Consumers travel further (1) takes time to find alternatives (1) less choice / variety (1) some products unavailable (1). Lower consumer confidence (1) lower welfare / living standards (1). Fewer external economies of scale (1) example (1) higher average cost (1) higher price (1). Focus must be on consumers; only one mark in total for higher price.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a government should encourage people to walk to school and work.
questions.ms:
Might: people healthier; higher productivity; lower healthcare costs; less pollution and traffic congestion; less need for car parking space.
Might not: may not be safe; people may be late; more stress, lower productivity; less demand for buses and trains; bus and train drivers may lose jobs; restricts job choice due to distance from home.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify the difference between microeconomics and macroeconomics.
questions.ms: Microeconomics is concerned with individual markets / decisions / firms / households (1). Macroeconomics is concerned with the whole economy (1).

questions.text: Explain how less education can reduce a person's lifetime earnings.
questions.ms: Logical explanation, 1 per link. Fewer qualifications (1) lower mobility (1) less chance of employment / more unemployment (1) may work in primary sector / manual work (1). Fewer skills / lower literacy (1) lower productivity (1) less chance of promotion (1). Less bargaining power / less aware of rights e.g. minimum wage (1) easier to replace (1). Less understanding of nutrition / healthcare (1) more time off work / shorter life (1). Larger families (1) out of labour force for a time (1). Less financial awareness / lower savings (1) can't buy equipment to raise earnings (1).

questions.text: Analyse how the introduction of a minimum wage could affect unemployment.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Minimum wage is the lowest wage an employer can pay / a price floor (1). Supply of labour may exceed demand / surplus of labour (1) so higher unemployment (1). Firms pay higher wages (1) raising costs of production (1) cutting profits (1) and output (1) so they fire workers (1) or replace workers with machines (1). BUT higher pay may raise productivity (1) and total demand (1) so firms raise output (1) and hire more (1) reducing cyclical unemployment (1). May increase incentive to work (1) reducing frictional unemployment (1). If set below equilibrium, no effect (1). One mark total for more / less unemployment; one mark total for output change.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not an economy with a high inflation rate will have a low economic growth rate.
questions.ms:
Might: products less internationally competitive; fewer exports, more imports; lower total demand; discourages investment; cost-push inflation reduces output; hyperinflation may collapse the economic system.
Might not: demand-pull inflation comes with rising demand, encouraging higher output / GDP; higher tax revenue can fund e.g. education, raising long-run growth; lowers the real cost of borrowing, boosting spending and investment; inflation may still be lower than rival countries'.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two reasons why tax revenue is likely to fall during a recession.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: lower spending / demand; lower incomes / wages / higher unemployment; lower profits; lower tax rates; lower imports; fewer taxpayers; lower output; lower revenue. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two characteristics of money.
questions.ms: 1 mark per characteristic + 1 per explanation. Generally acceptable (1) people willing to accept it as payment (1); portable (1) easy to carry (1); recognisable (1) easy to see it is the country's currency (1); durable (1) lasts / can be saved (1); limited in supply (1) so keeps value (1); divisible (1) units of different values (1); homogeneous / uniform (1) no preference between notes of the same value (1).

questions.text: Analyse the advantages an economy may gain from having some of its people working in other countries.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Workers send money home (1) reducing poverty / raising living standards (1). Improves current account / brings in foreign currency (1) as secondary income (1). Workers gain training / skills / knowledge of new technology / experience (1) higher productivity (1) which they bring back (1) raising quality of output (1). May start firms on return (1) raising output / GDP (1). May reduce unemployment (1) if there's a lack of jobs at home (1) cutting spending on unemployment benefits (1). No marks for general benefits of emigration.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not consumers would benefit from firms buying new capital equipment.
questions.ms:
Might: new technology; more innovation / new products; higher efficiency / lower costs; lower prices; fewer mistakes, better quality; more output and availability.
Might not: prices may rise short run to cover the cost; quality / output may fall short run as workers adapt; firms may switch from consumer to capital goods; products may become more standardised. Focus must be on consumers, not workers.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two free goods.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2, e.g. air / oxygen; sunlight; seawater / rain water; wind. BOD for sun, trees (not wood), wild flowers, wild fruit. Not fish or stone.
questions.subtopic: 1.1 The nature of the basic economic problem

questions.text: Explain two influences on demand for factors of production.
questions.ms: 1 mark per influence + 1 per explanation. Demand for the product / derived demand (1) more demand for the product raises demand for factors (1); price of the factor (1) lower price, higher demand (1); price of substitute factors (1) e.g. more labour if capital price rises (1); price of complementary factors (1) cheaper capital may raise demand for labour used with it (1); productivity (1) higher productivity raises demand (1); quality / technology / training (1); occupational mobility (1); method of production (1) switching away from labour-intensive raises demand for capital (1).

questions.text: Analyse the effect of an increase in demand for football shirts on demand for football shorts and demand for basketball shirts.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis. Demand for football shorts likely to increase (1) as shirts and shorts are complements (1) bought / used together (1). Demand for basketball shirts likely to fall (1) as they may be substitutes (1) consumers switch between them (1). Changes may be shown on diagrams.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not an increase in government spending on housing would benefit an economy.
questions.ms:
Might: raises total demand; raises output / GDP; more employment, less unemployment; lower house prices; higher living standards; less homelessness and poverty.
Might not: opportunity cost; may mean higher taxes; housing quality may be low; private sector may provide better housing; external costs during construction.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text:
Economists describe resources as being ‘scarce’.
What must be a consequence of scarce resources?
questions.ms: Answer: D (wants will exceed productive capacity)
questions.subtopic: 1.1 The nature of the basic economic problem

questions.text:
The diagram shows the production possibility curve (PPC) for an economy producing consumer goods and capital goods.
The economy is currently producing OM consumer goods and OG capital goods. It decides to increase production of capital goods to OH.
What is the opportunity cost of this decision in terms of consumer goods?
questions.ms: Answer: B (ML)

questions.text:
A hospital has spent all of its budget allocated for employing doctors.
What is the opportunity cost to the hospital of employing an extra doctor?
options: a reduction in the number of nurses employed
an improvement in the recovery rate of patients
an increase in the number of patients treated
the salary paid to the extra doctor
questions.ms: Answer: A (a reduction in the number of nurses employed)

questions.text:
There has been an increase in the demand for wheat. This has led to an increase in the demand for labour to harvest the wheat.
Which branch of economics covers these two concepts?
(increase in the demand for wheat | increase in the demand for labour to harvest wheat)
questions.ms: Answer: D (microeconomics | microeconomics)

questions.text:
In the United Kingdom (UK), the price of timber used in house building increased. This was because of a boom in the UK house building industry and a shortage of drivers to deliver the timber.
What happened in the UK market for timber to cause this price increase?
(demand curve | supply curve)
questions.ms: Answer: C (shifted right | shifted left)

questions.text: What does a supply curve show?
options: A firm will supply more when consumers’ purchasing power increases.
The higher the price, the fewer goods are supplied as costs of production increase.
The lower the price, the more profit is made by the firm.
There is a positive relationship between quantity supplied and price.
questions.ms: Answer: D (There is a positive relationship between quantity supplied and price.)

questions.text:
A global pandemic causes the demand for air travel to decrease.
Which value for the price elasticity of supply of air travel will cause the number of tickets for air travel to fall the most?
questions.ms: Answer: D (1.5)

questions.text: What is a disadvantage of a market economy?
questions.ms: Answer: B (not enough merit goods)

questions.text:
Droughts in some countries caused the supply of wheat to fall. Wheat prices then rose providing an opportunity for wheat producers in other countries to increase supply.
Why might the price of wheat continue to be high in the year following the drought?
options: Different weather conditions allowed a bumper harvest.
Suppliers unaffected by drought failed to increase output.
The government introduced a subsidy to wheat producers.
The wheat market returned to its original equilibrium.
questions.ms: Answer: B (Suppliers unaffected by drought failed to increase output.)

questions.text:
Newly built houses tend to be inelastic in supply. A government aim is to make the supply more elastic by relaxing building regulations.
Why is the government not likely to achieve this aim immediately?
options: Banks will only lend to high-income earners.
Costs of building materials fluctuate according to season.
Houses take a long period of time to be built.
Population increases lead to greater housing demand.
questions.ms: Answer: C (Houses take a long period of time to be built.)

questions.text:
A person planning for old age saves in the form of money rather than goods.
Which function does money perform when this is done?
questions.ms: Answer: C (store of value)

questions.text: What is not normally a function of the central bank of a country?
options: acting as lender of last resort
questions.ms: Answer: D (setting the government budget)

questions.text: What is a trade union most likely to protect?
options: the rights of a group of workers
questions.ms: Answer: B (the rights of a group of workers)

questions.text:
A person sets up a street food stall.
What is necessary for the food stall to survive in the long run?
(growth | profitability)
questions.ms: Answer: B (no | yes)

questions.text:
A large privately owned firm is the sole supplier of electricity to a city.
Which combination of characteristics is likely to exist for this firm?
(barriers to entry | long-run profit | pricing decision)
questions.ms: Answer: A (high | high | price maker)

questions.text:
When a firm produces 200 units, its total variable cost is $600 and its total fixed cost is $2000.
What is the average cost at this output?
questions.ms: Answer: C ($13)

questions.text:
The government of country Z announces a forecast budget deficit of $234 billion, as part of its fiscal policy.
What is the effect of this forecast budget deficit likely to be?
questions.ms: Answer: C (an increase in employment)

questions.text:
Low-income groups do not pay income tax but are able to use state-provided healthcare services.
What does this illustrate?
questions.ms: Answer: C (redistribution of income)

questions.text:
The government uses monetary policy and reduces the interest rate.
What might be a consequence of this?
options: a decrease in the rate of inflation
an increase in the level of investment
an increase in the level of savings
questions.ms: Answer: B (an increase in the level of investment)

questions.text: What is a likely objective of supply-side policy?
options: increasing the power of trade unions
questions.ms: Answer: A (improving productive potential)

questions.text: An increase in which economic indicator best describes economic growth?
questions.ms: Answer: C (level of output)

questions.text: What is full employment considered to be?
questions.ms: Answer: A (no cyclical unemployment)

questions.text: Which group is most likely to benefit during a period of rapid inflation?
questions.ms: Answer: C (people with debts)

questions.text: What are the components of the Human Development Index (HDI)?
options: life expectancy at birth, expected years of schooling, gross national income (GNI)
life expectancy at birth, expected years of schooling, gross national income (GNI) per head
population growth, adult literacy rate, gross national income (GNI) per head
population size, expected years of schooling, number of doctors per head
