questions.ms: Answer: B (life expectancy at birth, expected years of schooling, gross national income (GNI) per head)

questions.text: Which situation must produce an ageing population?
options: a falling birth rate and a falling death rate
a rising birth rate and a rising death rate
a rising marriage rate and a falling death rate
a falling marriage rate and a rising death rate
questions.ms: Answer: A (a falling birth rate and a falling death rate)

questions.text:
The table shows the unemployment rate in three developed economies in one year.
What is the main cause of high rates of unemployment in developed economies in periods of recession?
questions.ms: Answer: A (decreases in total demand)

questions.text: What is most likely to result from an extension of specialisation in manufacturing?
options: for the consumer some prices will be reduced
for the country there will be less dependency on international trade
for the employee the work will become more varied
for the producer there will be less efficiency
questions.ms: Answer: A (for the consumer some prices will be reduced)

questions.text:
A country imposes a tariff on an imported product.
What is the effect of this change?
(the price of the product increases | the quantity of the product imported is fixed)
questions.ms: Answer: C (yes | no)

questions.text:
The world demand for oil is price-inelastic and oil is paid for in US dollars.
If the price of oil falls rapidly, how might it affect the US dollar?
(market for US$ | exchange rate for US$)
questions.ms: Answer: C (less demand for US$ | decreases)

questions.text: Which benefit do multinational companies (MNCs) bring to their home country?
questions.ms: Answer: A (flow of profits)

questions.text: Which statement is correct?
options: Economic goods have no opportunity cost.
Free goods have no opportunity cost.
questions.ms: Answer: D (Free goods have no opportunity cost.)
questions.subtopic: 1.1 The nature of the basic economic problem

questions.text:
The economy of country X is always on its production possibility curve (PPC).
When will the goods and services produced by country X become more scarce?
(PPC | population size)
questions.ms: Answer: A (shifts left | increases)

questions.text: What is capital?
options: the ability to organise the factors of production
the money invested in a firm
questions.ms: Answer: C (the factory used in production)

questions.text:
What are features of a market economy?
(private ownership of factors of production | government allocation of production | public ownership of factors of production)
questions.ms: Answer: C (yes | no | no)

questions.text:
Public transport and cars are substitute goods. The price of public transport rises.
What will happen to the demand for cars?
questions.ms: Answer: D (It will increase.)

questions.text:
The markets of four products are all in equilibrium. The demand for each product shifts to the right by 5000 units at all prices.
Which product will have the largest price increase? (value of price elasticity of supply shown)
questions.ms: Answer: A (PES = 0)

questions.text: What is the value of the price elasticity of demand (PED) for a product if total revenue remains the same when the price is reduced?
questions.ms: Answer: D (1)

questions.text:
The owner of a hotel in Malaysia finds that the price elasticity of demand (PED) for accommodation in the area is –1.7.
If the hotel owner decreases the price of a room by 5%, how would the demand for a room change?
questions.ms: Answer: D (It would increase by 8.5%.)

questions.text:
Good weather results in an increase in the demand for tomatoes. It also increases the supply of tomatoes.
What must be a result of this?
options: The price of tomatoes will fall.
The price of tomatoes will rise.
The quantity of tomatoes traded will fall.
The quantity of tomatoes traded will rise.
questions.ms: Answer: D (The quantity of tomatoes traded will rise.)

questions.text: What causes a change in the price of a product in a free market economy?
options: changes in demand and supply conditions
changes in external costs and external benefits
changes in the quantity of public goods
questions.ms: Answer: A (changes in demand and supply conditions)

questions.text:
The ways of making and receiving payments continue to develop. Payments can now be made using smartphones, as well as cash, debit cards and credit cards.
Which method of paying for products provides no information to sellers about their customers?
questions.ms: Answer: A (cash)

questions.text: In most countries, which organisation controls the banking system?
questions.ms: Answer: A (central bank)

questions.text: What is not a reason for differences in the earnings of airline pilots in a particular country?
questions.ms: Answer: D (inflation)

questions.text:
An airline takes over an online clothing company.
What is an advantage of such a move by the airline?
questions.ms: Answer: A (to diversify their operations)

questions.text:
In which type of industry is a firm most likely to make a large profit in the short run and in the long run?
(number of firms in the industry | barriers to entry into the industry)
questions.ms: Answer: C (one | high)

questions.text:
A firm produces five units of output at an average cost of $20 per unit. The cost of the sixth unit is $26.
What is the average cost of six units?
questions.ms: Answer: D ($21)

questions.text: What is an example of government macroeconomic policy?
options: preventing price rises in the food industry
removing a monopoly's barriers to entry
setting a maximum price for wheat
questions.ms: Answer: A (increasing the money supply)

questions.text: Why would devaluing the international value of an economy's currency help reduce unemployment?
options: Devaluing the currency would increase the cost of production.
Devaluing the currency would increase the confidence of investors.
Devaluing the currency would increase the foreign demand for domestic products.
Devaluing the currency would increase the demand for imports.
questions.ms: Answer: C (Devaluing the currency would increase the foreign demand for domestic products.)

questions.text: What is likely to happen when the rate of interest increases?
questions.ms: Answer: B (firms buy fewer machines)

questions.text: What is not a supply-side policy measure?
questions.ms: Answer: B (higher indirect taxation)

questions.text:
The real GDP per head for a country was $20 000 in 2021 and $21 000 in 2022.
What is most likely to have changed between 2021 and 2022?
options: There was more activity in the informal economy.
The living standards of some people improved.
questions.ms: Answer: C (The living standards of some people improved.)

questions.text: Which change to fiscal policy is most likely to reduce cyclical unemployment in an economy?
questions.ms: Answer: B (increasing the budget deficit)

questions.text: What must have happened in a country when it experienced an annual rate of inflation of 100%?
options: The purchasing power of money halved.
The real value of money doubled.
questions.ms: Answer: C (The purchasing power of money halved.)

questions.text:
The Human Development Index (HDI) can be used to measure human development in countries.
Which measure would not be part of its calculation?
questions.ms: Answer: A (inequality of incomes)

questions.text: What is the most likely consequence of an ageing population for a high-income economy?
options: There will be a fall in the dependency ratio.
There will be a fall in the level of immigration.
There will be an increase in geographic mobility.
There will be an increase in spending on healthcare.
questions.ms: Answer: D (There will be an increase in spending on healthcare.)

questions.text:
In some developing countries a large percentage of the population is involved in subsistence farming.
What can be concluded from this?
options: Each family will be able to produce enough to live on.
Production is unlikely to be capital intensive.
There will be a high level of trade.
questions.ms: Answer: B (Production is unlikely to be capital intensive.)
questions.subtopic: 5.4 Differences in economic development between countries

questions.text:
A small country whose only export is oil decides to reduce substantially the rate at which it extracts its limited oil reserves.
What is the most likely reason for this decision?
options: to improve the balance of payments in the following year
to raise the level of employment in the oil industry
questions.ms: Answer: C (to maintain future living standards)

questions.text:
Country X believes that country Y is selling steel at prices below the average cost of production. So, country X imposes a higher tariff on steel imports from country Y.
What does country X hope to achieve by imposing this higher tariff?
options: avoid country X dumping steel in country Y
avoid country Y dumping steel in country X
questions.ms: Answer: B (avoid country Y dumping steel in country X)

questions.text: Which factor would cause a country's exchange rate to fall?
questions.ms: Answer: A (Demand for imports increases.)

questions.text:
Many European firms employ workers from the Philippines. These workers send part of their income to relatives in the Philippines.
In which part of the balance of payments current account for the Philippines would these transactions be recorded?
questions.ms: Answer: B (secondary income)
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text:
A consumer has $10 to spend. A meal costs $9 and a drink costs $5.
What would describe the situation if the consumer did not have enough money to purchase both the meal and the drink?
questions.ms: Answer: D (the economic problem)
questions.subtopic: 1.1 The nature of the basic economic problem

questions.text:
The diagram shows a production possibility curve (PPC) for a country. The country moved from position X to position Y on the PPC.
What is the most likely reason for this change?
options: Firms have decided to increase investment in technology.
New economic resources have been discovered in the country.
The government has brought about an increase in living standards.
The government has encouraged long-term economic growth.
questions.ms: Answer: C (The government has brought about an increase in living standards.)

questions.text: Which type of factor of production is a railway track?
questions.ms: Answer: A (capital)

questions.text: Which statement must be correct if a market is in disequilibrium?
options: Quantity demanded and quantity supplied are equal.
The government must intervene if anything is to be sold.
There can be no changes to demand or supply.
There is excess supply or excess demand.
questions.ms: Answer: D (There is excess supply or excess demand.)

questions.text: What is a determinant of price elasticity of demand (PED)?
options: availability of stocks of the product
change in the income of consumers
degree of necessity of the product
questions.ms: Answer: C (degree of necessity of the product)

questions.text: What would cause the supply curve for an agricultural product to shift to the right?
options: an increase in the costs of production
an increase in the price of substitutes
an increase in the price of the good
an increase in the productivity of farms
questions.ms: Answer: D (an increase in the productivity of farms)

questions.text: What would increase the price elasticity of supply (PES) of a product?
options: an increase in the cost of inputs
an increase in the firm’s profits
an increase in the number of close substitutes
an increase in the time a product can be stored
questions.ms: Answer: D (an increase in the time a product can be stored)

questions.text:
The diagram shows a demand curve.
What does the movement from X to Y show?
options: a decrease in quantity demanded due to an increase in price
a decrease in quantity demanded due to changes in the conditions of demand
an increase in quantity demanded due to changes in the conditions of demand
an increase in quantity demanded due to an increase in price
questions.ms: Answer: A (a decrease in quantity demanded due to an increase in price)

questions.text:
In a market there is a surplus of a good.
Which change would cause the market to come to an equilibrium?
questions.ms: Answer: B (a fall in price)

questions.text:
When the price of a good is $10, the quantity demanded is 100 units per day.
Which combination of price change and price elasticity of demand will cause the largest increase in the quantity demanded for the good?
(price change | price elasticity of demand)
questions.ms: Answer: B (price falls to $9 | 1.2)

questions.text:
A function of money is to act as a measure of value.
What does this mean?
options: It is used for future savings.
It is used to compare the worth of different goods.
It is used to enable monthly payments for expensive goods.
It is used to pay the price of a good.
questions.ms: Answer: B (It is used to compare the worth of different goods.)

questions.text:
In 2008–2009 the central bank of a developed country reduced interest rates from 5% to 0.5% per year to stimulate the economy.
How would this policy have affected the amount saved and the cost of borrowing by individuals?
(amount saved | cost of borrowing)
questions.ms: Answer: A (decreased | decreased)

questions.text:
Many small energy providers have closed down due to rising costs.
What is the likely effect of this on the price of energy and choice of energy providers for consumers, assuming there is no government intervention?
(price of energy | choice of energy providers)
questions.ms: Answer: C (increases | decreases)

questions.text: What is the most likely goal of a state-owned enterprise providing health services?
questions.ms: Answer: B (public satisfaction)

questions.text:
Some governments allow monopoly markets to exist.
What is a reason for this?
options: to attract entry into the market
questions.ms: Answer: B (to fund research and development)

questions.text:
The table shows the costs incurred by a firm producing computers.
What are the fixed costs if 3000 computers are produced?
questions.ms: Answer: A ($20 000)

questions.text:
A government increases its revenue by higher direct taxation of both personal incomes and company profits.
What is most likely to be the reason for this increase?
options: to control spending on specific consumer goods
to provide public and merit goods
to reduce pollution from industrial production
questions.ms: Answer: C (to provide public and merit goods)

questions.text:
Income tax in a country gives all individuals an initial tax-free income allowance. Any income above this allowance is taxed at increasing rates as the incomes of individuals rise.
Which change to this income tax will be regressive?
options: decreasing the lowest rate of tax
increasing the top rate of tax
questions.ms: Answer: B (decreasing the tax-free income allowance)

questions.text:
A government lowers the rate of interest.
Who is most likely to be disadvantaged by this policy?
questions.ms: Answer: D (savers)

questions.text: What is a supply-side policy measure?
options: the removal of barriers to entry to a market
questions.ms: Answer: D (the removal of barriers to entry to a market)

questions.text: What is the most likely consequence of economic growth?
questions.ms: Answer: B (more use of resources)

questions.text:
In high-income economies, cereal farming is highly productive but few workers are employed.
What could have caused this employment situation?
options: a fall in world demand for cereals
questions.ms: Answer: C (increased mechanisation of agriculture)

questions.text: Who is most likely to benefit during a period of inflation?
questions.ms: Answer: B (debtors (borrowers))

questions.text:
The table shows some economic indicators.
Which increase in the first indicator is most likely to lead to an increase in the second indicator?
(first indicator | second indicator)
questions.ms: Answer: D (productivity | living standards)

questions.text:
Which combination would be most likely to increase the population of a country?
(birth rates | death rates | net immigration)
questions.ms: Answer: B (high | low | positive)

questions.text: Which economic consequence is most likely to result from an increasing proportion of the population being over the age of 65?
options: More facilities will be needed to retrain workers.
The total savings in the economy will increase.
There will be a rise in the economic growth rate.
questions.ms: Answer: A (Government transfer payments will increase.)

questions.text: What is most likely to encourage international specialisation?
options: similarities in climate in different countries
the ability to produce products more cheaply than other countries
the discovery of oil in a country that had no oil before
questions.ms: Answer: B (the ability to produce products more cheaply than other countries)

questions.text:
Country X established free trade agreements with other nations.
What would be the intended benefit of such agreements to country X?
questions.ms: Answer: C (more efficient allocation of resources)

questions.text:
A country’s foreign exchange rate appreciates significantly.
Which group in the country will directly benefit from this change?
options: a government department which only buys locally made goods
retailers who get all their supplies from foreign producers
workers in local companies that compete with foreign firms in the local market
workers in local companies that sell only in foreign countries
questions.ms: Answer: B (retailers who get all their supplies from foreign producers)

questions.text: What is measured in the secondary income balance in a country’s current account of the balance of payments?
options: net contributions to international and regional organisations
net exports of goods and services
net inflow of income from factors of production abroad
questions.ms: Answer: A (net contributions to international and regional organisations)
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text: Calculate the total number of people in Cambridge aged 18–29 in 2019.
questions.ms: 1 mark: 37,440 (30% of 124,800). Correct answer with no working gets full credit.

questions.text: Identify two types of industries in Cambridge that operate in the tertiary sector.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: education; healthcare; research and development. If more than two are given, consider only the first three. Hi-tech manufacturing is NOT tertiary.

questions.text: Identify two benefits of having highly knowledge-intensive exports.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: exports are highly priced / high value; demand is price inelastic; demand for exports rises as global incomes rise. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain how having a more educated labour force can reduce poverty.
questions.ms: 4 marks for a logical chain of explanation, 1 mark per developed link. Examples: more skilled / more productive (1) so can earn higher wages (1) so can afford basic necessities (1). More job opportunities / less unemployment (1) wages higher than unemployment benefits (1). Better access to health information (1) so more able to work (1) and access better healthcare (1).

questions.text:
Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effects of increased global income on the market for education in Cambridge.
(Describe your diagram in words: axes, original curves, which curve shifts and which way, and the old and new equilibrium price and quantity.)
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 4: axes labelled price and quantity (1); original demand and supply curves labelled (1); DEMAND curve shifts to the right (1); equilibria shown, P1/Q1 and P2/Q2 or E1 and E2, with higher price and higher quantity (1). A supply shift earns no mark for the shift.

questions.text: Analyse the relationship between the percentage of population aged 25–64 with a university degree and GDP per head.
questions.ms: 5 marks. Expected relationship: positive / direct relationship (1), higher % with degree, higher GDP per head (1). Analysis of why: more skills / qualifications (1) so higher productivity and higher earnings (1). Supporting evidence from table, e.g. Indonesia lowest in both; Canada, Switzerland, UK highest three in both; Colombia second lowest in both (up to 2). Exception: Switzerland (1) has a lower % with a degree than Canada or UK but higher GDP per head (1). Analysis of exception: other influences e.g. quality of secondary education, share of population in banking (1). Answer does not need this exact structure but should cover relationship, evidence, exception and analysis.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not free trade is beneficial for a city such as Cambridge.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for reasons it might be beneficial, up to 4 for reasons it might not, max 6 total.
Might: easier to export (1) higher export revenue (1) higher profits (1) growth in the city (1); cheaper imported materials (1) lower costs / prices (1); more jobs (1) lower unemployment (1); bigger market (1) economies of scale (1); more consumer choice / quality from imports (1); more competition or transfer of ideas (1) more innovation / lower prices (1); encourages entrepreneurship / investment (1).
Might not: overdependence on foreign markets (1) shocks abroad cut firms' revenues (1) lower growth (1); cheaper foreign competitors / more imports (1) hurts infant industries (1) job losses (1); gains go to certain firms / workers only (1) more inequality (1); more production and transport (1) more pollution / negative externalities (1); more demerit goods (1) worse health (1); global monopolies (1) smaller domestic firms cannot compete (1).
A reason on one side that is simply the reverse of a reason already credited on the other side earns 0.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not firms in Cambridge will continue to grow.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for reasons they might grow, up to 4 for reasons they might not, max 6 total.
Might: access to many highly skilled, educated workers from around the world (1) easy to recruit (1) to produce output (1); skilled workers are more productive (1) more innovation / higher quality (1); young workers up to date with technology (1); good infrastructure e.g. ultra-fast broadband (1) higher productivity / fewer delays (1); good transport links and airports (1) easier to export / reach customers (1) faster deliveries (1) higher demand (1).
Might not: high land and office costs (1) high production costs (1) lower profits (1); high house prices / poor air quality (1) put workers off moving to Cambridge (1) hard to recruit (1); small population (1) small local market (1) limited demand / revenue (1); overdependence on one sector e.g. education (1) limits growth elsewhere (1); skilled workers are available in other cities too (1).
Pure reverse arguments earn 0.

questions.text: State how average revenue is calculated.
questions.ms: Total revenue (1) divided by quantity sold (1). Accept "quantity" without "sold".

questions.text: Explain two advantages of a large firm.
questions.ms: 1 mark per advantage identified (max 2) + 1 mark per explanation (max 2). Examples: economies of scale (1) lower average cost than small firms (1); easier access to finance (1) e.g. bank loans (1); technological development (1) higher productivity (1); large customer base (1) higher revenue / profit (1); well known (1) brand loyalty (1). Two different economies of scale can count as two advantages.

questions.text: Analyse the possible causes of higher prices of a product such as ski holidays in the Alps.
questions.ms: 6 marks for coherent analysis, 1 per developed point. Higher demand / popularity (1) from advertising / reputation / higher quality / higher price of substitute holidays (1); more price-inelastic demand (1) less responsive to price, e.g. brand loyalty (1); higher incomes of target market (1) luxury good (1); lower supply (1); more inelastic supply (1) e.g. regulations (1); higher production costs (1) e.g. higher labour costs / minimum wage / living costs of workers (1); investment in facilities e.g. ski lifts (1) raising short-run costs (1). A fall in the price of a complement (e.g. ski equipment) raising demand is also accepted.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not government intervention is beneficial for firms.
questions.ms:
Levels-based.
Might: subsidies cut costs / help survival in crises; lower taxes cut production costs; minimum prices raise revenue; education spending raises worker skills; benefits spending raises demand; anti-monopoly regulation promotes competition.
Might not: regulations raise costs; minimum wage raises costs, cuts profit; direct / indirect taxes cut profits; maximum prices cut revenue; trade restrictions limit competition.

questions.text: Identify two types of tax.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: direct; indirect; progressive; proportional; regressive. Accept real examples e.g. income tax, tariffs. Accept specific / ad valorem.

questions.text: Explain two functions of money.
questions.ms: 1 mark per function identified (max 2) + 1 per explanation (max 2). Medium of exchange (1) used to buy goods and services / trade (1); measure of value / unit of account (1) shows what a product is worth (1); store of value (1) lets people save (1); standard of deferred payment (1) enables borrowing and lending (1).

questions.text: Analyse the consequences of market failure.
questions.ms: 6 marks for coherent analysis. Market failure = inefficient production / consumption (1); overconsumption of demerit goods (1) and goods with external costs (1) misallocation of resources (1) e.g. cigarettes, fossil fuels (1); underconsumption of merit goods (1) and goods with external benefits (1) e.g. education, healthcare (1); public goods not supplied (1) e.g. defence (1); abuse of monopoly power (1) higher prices (1) less affordability / choice (1); factor immobility (1) shortages and surpluses (1) unemployment (1) lower income / poverty (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a tax on a product can reduce external costs.
questions.ms:
Levels-based.
Might: tax raises price so quantity demanded falls; if demand is price elastic, quantity falls a lot; tax raises production costs so supply falls; tax cuts firms' profits; revenue can fund subsidies for less-polluting products.
Might not: tax is small relative to final price; avoidance / evasion / illegal markets; if demand is price inelastic (e.g. addictive products), quantity barely falls.

questions.text: Identify, other than natural rubber, two primary-sector products.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2, e.g. coal, oil, fish, wood, wheat. Accept a process e.g. fishing. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two reasons why a country may change its specialisation.
questions.ms: 1 mark per reason (max 2) + 1 per explanation (max 2). Change in quantity / quality of resources (1) e.g. discovery of resources or new technology (1), other countries more / less efficient (1); change in production costs (1) e.g. higher minimum wage or cheaper technology (1); change in demand / consumer behaviour (1) changing revenue / profits (1); change in competition (1) other countries gain competitive advantage (1).

questions.text: Analyse the economic benefits for a country in producing manufactured goods instead of primary-sector products.
questions.ms: 6 marks for coherent analysis. Higher prices / higher value added (1) higher revenue / profit (1); more exports (1) higher total demand (1) economic growth (1); higher productivity (1) economies of scale (1); more demand for workers (1) lower unemployment (1) more skilled jobs (1) higher incomes / living standards / less poverty (1); no need for a stock of natural resources (1) skills and technology can be learned / imported (1); less dependent on weather (1) more stable income (1) easier to plan (1); higher tax revenue (1) more government spending on healthcare, education, infrastructure (1) more development (1).
questions.subtopic: 5.4 Differences in economic development between countries

questions.text: Discuss whether or not labour-intensive production will harm an economy.
questions.ms:
Levels-based.
Might harm: labour may cost more than capital; less reliable / consistent; trade unions may cause disruption; lower productivity; needs breaks; less cost-effective so lower international competitiveness.
Might not: high employment and living standards; lower unemployment so less spent on benefits; labour is more flexible than machines (can retrain, move, change output); workers respond better to customers.

questions.text: Identify two monetary policy measures.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: changes in interest rates; money supply (accept quantitative easing); foreign exchange rate. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two microeconomic policy measures that can be taken by a government to reduce the price of a product.
questions.ms: 1 mark per measure (max 2) + 1 per explanation (max 2). Maximum prices (1) e.g. rent controls (1); subsidies (1) lower production costs (1); nationalisation (1) government sets lower prices (1); direct provision (1) raises supply e.g. public housing (1); regulation (1) e.g. banning foreign house buying to cut demand (1); deregulation (1) more firms / competition (1); lower sales taxes (1) if passed on as lower prices (1). Examples can be from any market.

questions.text: Analyse the key determinants of price elasticity of supply of a product.
questions.ms: 6 marks for coherent analysis. Stocks (1) unsold finished goods (1) high stocks mean elastic supply (1); spare capacity (1) unused factors e.g. workers not full time (1) more spare capacity means more elastic (1); time period (1) short run vs long run (1) short run inelastic (1) because at least one factor is fixed (1) making it harder to raise output (1), long run elastic (1) all factors variable (1); difficulty / length of production (1) easy-to-make goods more elastic (1) e.g. bread vs smartphone (1). An approach explaining why PES may be inelastic is also accepted.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not trade unions benefit workers.
questions.ms:
Levels-based.
Might: collective bargaining can raise wages; better hours and conditions; more job security; lobby government for worker-friendly policy e.g. maternity pay; provide services e.g. training.
Might not: higher wages raise costs so firms cut jobs; strikes cut productivity and workers' pay; lower competitiveness reduces investment and demand for labour; workers may disagree with union aims; membership fees may outweigh benefits.

questions.text: Calculate what percentage of Honduran people did not have access to electricity in 2020.
questions.ms: 1 mark: 8.3% (accept 8 or 8.3).

questions.text: Identify two benefits the Honduran economy could gain from a growth in the US economy.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: sell more exports to the US; receive more money sent home by Honduran workers in the US; more job opportunities for Hondurans in the US. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain one advantage of an economy specialising.
questions.ms: 1 mark for the advantage (from the source) + 1 for explanation. Gains skills (1) so higher productivity / efficiency / lower costs / higher quality / more output (1). Gains a good reputation (1) so higher demand (1).

questions.text: Explain two ways a government could redistribute income.
questions.ms: 1 mark per way (max 2) + 1 per explanation (max 2). Benefits e.g. unemployment / welfare benefit (1) raise income of those on low or no income / reduce absolute poverty (1). Progressive income tax (1) takes a higher proportion of income from the rich / revenue used to help the poor (1). "Tax the rich and give to the poor" alone = 1 mark.

questions.text: Draw a demand and supply diagram to show how a report stating that bananas are good for health would affect the market for bananas.
questions.ms: 1 each: axes labelled price and quantity (1); original D and S labelled (1); demand curve shifts right (1); equilibria shown P1/Q1 and P2/Q2 or E1/E2 (1).

questions.text: Analyse the relationship between the percentage of population living in poverty and life expectancy.
questions.ms: Inverse / negative relationship (1): higher poverty, lower life expectancy (1). Evidence: Sweden lowest poverty and highest life expectancy (1); Chad and South Sudan highest poverty and lowest life expectancy (1). Analysis: high poverty means poor healthcare / nutrition / housing / sanitation / education (1). Exception: Chad vs South Sudan (1), Chad has lower poverty but also lower life expectancy (1). Analysis of exception: other influences e.g. wars (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not the cost of producing clothes in Honduras will fall in the future.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 each side, max 6.
Might: more training (1) better working conditions (1) higher productivity / skills (1) lower labour costs (1); more capital goods (1) fewer mistakes / less waste (1) faster production / higher productivity (1); better conditions (1) less industrial action / more motivation (1); firms grow (1) economies of scale (1).
Might not: raw material prices may rise (1) bad weather / falling exchange rate / tariffs on imported materials (1) reduce supply (1); falling unemployment (1) harder to recruit (1) stronger worker bargaining power (1) higher wages (1); training and better conditions cost money (1); capital goods need high initial spending (1); diseconomies of scale (1); higher taxes on clothes firms (1). Reverse arguments earn 0.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a fall in unemployment in Honduras is likely to cause inflation.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 each side, max 6.
Might: unemployment already low (1) nearing full employment (1) pushes up wages (1) higher costs (1) cost-push inflation (1); higher incomes (1) more consumer spending (1) higher total demand (1) demand-pull inflation (1); inflation already exists (1) workers expect it to continue (1) higher wage claims (1).
Might not: higher investment (1) total supply rises with total demand (1); less spent on benefits (1) more tax revenue (1) smaller budget deficit (1) slower growth in total demand (1); extra income saved / spent on imports (1) due to uncertainty (1); fall in unemployment may not mean more employment, e.g. retired / emigrated (1).

questions.text: Define, with an example, a capital good.
questions.ms: A good used to produce other goods or services / human-made good used in production (1) e.g. a machine (1).

questions.text: Explain two reasons why a low inflation rate may increase a country's economic growth rate.
questions.ms: 1 per reason (max 2) + 1 per explanation (max 2). Products more internationally competitive (1) more exports / fewer imports (1); more certainty (1) encourages investment / attracts MNCs (1); keeps cost increases low (1) fewer claims for higher wages (1); more confidence (1) higher demand / profits (1).

questions.text: Analyse how a government could reduce protectionism and move towards free international trade.
questions.ms: Remove tariffs (1) cheaper imports (1) domestic firms with lower costs can compete (1); remove / raise quotas (1) remove bans / embargoes (1) more imports allowed (1); remove subsidies (1) products no longer artificially cheap (1); other countries may remove their protection too (1) exports sold without restriction (1). Also reward deregulation, less bureaucracy, removing voluntary export restraints.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a country will benefit from diamond mining.
questions.ms:
Levels-based.
Might: high global demand; improves current account; creates skilled and unskilled jobs; higher output / economic growth; more tax revenue.
Might not: demand falls in a recession; price fluctuates; competition; accidents; external costs e.g. pollution; MNC profits sent abroad; supply gets depleted; better to conserve if prices rise later; may be a small share of GDP.

questions.text: Define, with an example, a fixed cost.
questions.ms: A cost that does not change with output / must be paid even when output is zero (1) e.g. rent (1). "A cost that does not change" alone is not enough.

questions.text: Explain two types of unemployment.
questions.ms: 1 per type (max 2) + 1 per explanation (max 2). Frictional (1) workers between jobs (1); structural (1) changes in demand / skills don't match vacancies / immobility (1); cyclical / demand-deficient (1) lack of total demand / recession (1). Also allow seasonal, regional, technological, voluntary, involuntary.

questions.text: Analyse how supply-side policy measures could reduce unemployment.
questions.ms: Education / training (1) more skills / productivity / mobility (1) reduces structural unemployment (1). Lower income tax / lower benefits (1) more incentive to find work (1) reduces frictional unemployment (1). Lower corporation tax (1) firms invest / expand (1). Privatisation / deregulation (1) more efficiency, lower costs (1) firms can afford more workers (1). Labour market reform (1) easier to hire (1). Infrastructure spending (1) lower costs / more mobility (1). Subsidies (1) firms expand (1). Better healthcare (1) less working time lost (1). Reward "raise productivity" only once.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not having fewer firms in a market will benefit consumers.
questions.ms:
Levels-based.
Might: bigger firms get economies of scale; lower costs mean lower prices; more profit reinvested in quality; firms may have left in response to changing demand; polluting firms may close; less time shopping around.
Might not: diseconomies of scale; less choice; less competition / move towards monopoly means higher prices and lower quality; lower availability.

questions.text: Define elastic supply.
questions.ms: 2 marks: percentage change in quantity supplied is greater than the percentage change in price. 1 mark: change in supply greater than change in price / PES > 1.

questions.text: Explain two reasons why a government may subsidise food production.
questions.ms: 1 per reason (max 2) + 1 per explanation (max 2). More output (1) overcome shortage (1); lower price (1) food more affordable / less poverty (1); better quality (1) better nutrition / health (1); higher farmer incomes (1) stop farms closing (1); fewer food imports / more exports (1) better current account / less dependence on other countries (1); more rural employment (1).

questions.text: Analyse what influences a farmer's demand for labour.
questions.ms: Demand for food (1) derived demand, more food demand means more workers (1). Wage rates (1) lower wages make workers cheaper (1). Skills (1) more skilled means more productive (1). Price of other factors (1) e.g. cheaper drones cut demand for labour (1). Technology (1) machinery may replace workers (1). Type of farming, labour vs capital intensive (1). Farm size (1). Subsidies (1) encourage expansion (1). Seasons (1) more labour at harvest (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not people living in cities have a higher living standard than those living in rural areas.
questions.ms:
Levels-based.
Might: more jobs; higher incomes; more entertainment; shorter distance to schools and shops; better access to healthcare; better quality education and healthcare.
Might not: traffic congestion; overcrowding; more air and noise pollution; higher stress; higher cost of living.

questions.text: Identify two benefits of a decrease in a country's population size.
questions.ms: 1 each, max 2: fewer dependents; less pressure on resources; less food needed; move towards optimum population; less overcrowding; less pollution; fewer imports; lower government spending on health / education; less unemployment; higher GDP per head.

questions.text: Explain how a market moves from disequilibrium to equilibrium.
questions.ms: Demand greater than supply / shortage (1) price rises (1). Supply greater than demand / surplus (1) price falls (1). Demand becomes equal to supply again (1). Max 2 for diagrams alone.

questions.text:
Analyse, using a production possibility curve (PPC) diagram, the effect of a decrease in the size of a country's labour force on its economy.
(Describe your diagram in words.)
questions.ms: Up to 4 for the diagram: axes labelled with two different goods (1); initial PPC drawn to the axes (1); new PPC drawn to the axes (1); shift to the LEFT shown (1). Up to 2 for analysis: fewer factors of production / resources (1) lower productive capacity / maximum output (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not an increase in exports will benefit an economy.
questions.ms:
Levels-based.
Might: more export revenue, better current account; higher total demand; more investment; economic growth; less unemployment; higher incomes.
Might not: demand-pull inflation; opportunity cost of selling less at home; shortages at home; resources depleted; higher exchange rate reverses the rise in exports; more exposed to external shocks.
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text: Calculate Montenegro's budget deficit as a percentage of its GDP.
Identify two examples of capital goods in Montenegro.
questions.ms: 1 mark each: computers; office buildings. Also accept e.g. telecommunications equipment, aluminium production factories.

questions.text: Explain one way price elasticity of demand may influence firms' decision making.
questions.ms: If demand is price elastic (1) firms know raising price will cut revenue / lowering price will raise revenue (1). No mark for identifying inelastic demand, but allow the second mark for explaining it (raising price raises revenue). Don't reward effects on demand or profit alone.

questions.text: Explain two ways the pattern of employment has changed in Montenegro in recent years.
questions.ms: 1 mark per change + 1 per reason. Higher proportion in tourism / the tertiary sector (1) due to growth of tourism / fewer in primary and secondary (1). More workers in the private sector, e.g. banking, telecommunications, aluminium (1) due to privatisation / fewer in the state sector (1).

questions.text: Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effect of a minimum price set above the equilibrium price on the market for oranges.
questions.ms: 1 mark each: axes labelled price and quantity (1); demand and supply curves labelled (1); minimum price line ABOVE equilibrium, labelled e.g. Pmin (not P2) (1); supply shown greater than demand e.g. Qd < Qs (1). No mark for the minimum price if a curve is also shifted.

questions.text: Analyse the relationship between countries' trade in goods and services balances and their current account balances.
questions.ms:
Approach A: positive relationship (1) a trade deficit tends to go with a current account deficit, a surplus with a surplus (1). Evidence: Bosnia & Herzegovina, Kosovo, Montenegro have deficits on both (1); Bulgaria, Slovenia surpluses on both (1). Exception: Croatia (1) trade deficit but current account surplus (1).
Approach B: no fixed relationship as the current account has other items (1). Five countries have a current account balance above their trade balance (1) e.g. (1). Exception: Slovenia (1) $4.6bn trade surplus but only $3.0bn current account (1).
Analysis (both, max 3): trade in goods and services is the largest component (1); the current account also includes primary and secondary income (1); five countries must have had a surplus on these (1); Slovenia a deficit (1). Max 5.
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text: Discuss whether or not privatisation is likely to have benefited consumers in Montenegro.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for might, up to 4 for might not, max 6. 1 mark for an accurate definition of privatisation.
Might: profit-driven firms (1) invest more / more R&D (1) better quality (1) lower costs (1); more firms enter (1) more competition (1) lower prices (1) more choice (1); respond faster (1) to changes in consumer demand (1).
Might not: state firms may have been subsidised (1) investment may now be lower (1); profit maximisers (1) may become monopolies (1) restrict supply (1) push up prices (1) lower quality (1) not everyone can afford (1); smaller firms (1) lose economies of scale (1); ignore external costs (1) e.g. pollution (1). Focus must be on consumers.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not deflation would benefit the Montenegro economy.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for would, up to 4 for would not, max 6. 1 mark for defining deflation (a fall in the price level).
Would: products more internationally competitive (1) more exports (1) fewer imports (1) smaller current account deficit (1); if caused by new technology / supply-side improvements (1) more output (1) and employment (1) growth / higher living standards (1).
Would not: inflation is only 0.4% (1); uncertainty (1) consumers and firms delay spending / investment (1) expecting further price falls (1); if caused by falling total demand (1) less output (1) recession (1) firms close (1) more unemployment (1) when it's already 18% (1); bigger budget deficit (1) from lower tax revenue (1) and more benefits (1).

questions.text: Identify two reasons why a person may experience absolute poverty.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: unemployment; sickness / poor health; old age; being a refugee; war / famine / natural disaster; lack of government benefits; low education / skills; income too low for basic necessities. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two causes of an increase in a country's economic development.
questions.ms: 1 mark per cause + 1 per explanation. Better education (1) more productive capacity, higher wages, less unemployment (1); better healthcare (1) longer life expectancy (1); better technology (1) better quality goods (1); more saving (1) finance for investment (1); more investment (1) growth (1); more FDI (1) more jobs (1); more tertiary sector workers (1) better pay / conditions (1); higher incomes (1) buy more goods (1); infrastructure spending (1) better labour mobility (1); more trade / exports (1) more jobs and income (1); new resources (1) e.g. oil (1). Consider first three only.
questions.subtopic: 5.4 Differences in economic development between countries

questions.text: Analyse, using a production possibility curve (PPC) diagram, the effect of a serious storm on an economy.
questions.ms: Diagram (up to 4): axes labelled with two different outputs (1); original PPC drawn touching both axes (1); new PPC drawn touching both axes (1); inward shift shown by an arrow or labels (1). Analysis (up to 2): the storm destroys resources / factors of production / infrastructure (1) reducing productive capacity / maximum output (1). Axes labelled only A and B are not enough.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not imposing tariffs on imports will increase a country's output.
questions.ms:
Might: imports become dearer, reducing demand for them; people switch to domestically produced products; net exports rise, raising total demand; higher demand encourages domestic firms to produce more; tariff revenue could subsidise domestic goods.
Might not: imports may still be cheaper than domestic products; there may be no domestic substitutes; tariffs on raw materials and capital goods raise production costs; other countries may retaliate, reducing demand for exports. Level 1 is just knowledge of imports and tariffs or identifying points.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two types of economic system.
questions.ms: 1 mark each: market; mixed. Also accept planned / command. No marks for 'free market' or 'controlled market' system.

questions.text: Explain two functions of a central bank.
questions.ms: 1 mark per function + 1 per explanation. Runs monetary policy / controls inflation (1) sets interest rates / manages money supply (1); quantitative easing (1) in a financial crisis (1); issues notes and coins (1); banker to the government (1) manages the national debt (1); lender of last resort (1) to commercial banks in difficulty (1); holds foreign currency reserves (1) to influence the exchange rate (1); regulates the banking system (1). Consider first three only.

questions.text: Analyse the advantages to a country of having a young population.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. More up to date with technology (1) more educated / skilled (1) more productive (1) more output (1). Adds to the labour force (1) more productive capacity (1) more tax revenue (1) for infrastructure (1). Less spending on pensions (1) and elderly healthcare (1) so more for education / infrastructure (1). More geographically mobile (1) fewer family ties (1). More occupationally mobile (1). Spend more (1) more innovative (1) start businesses (1). Fitter (1) less sickness absence (1). Attracts FDI (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a ban on cars in a city will benefit the city's households and firms.
questions.ms:
Might: less air and noise pollution; no traffic congestion; less staff illness; fewer accidents; more demand for and jobs in public transport; pedestrianised shopping areas attract customers; frees police and court time; better quality of life; frees funds for education, health, housing.
Might not: longer journeys by e.g. bike; people enjoy driving; fewer visitors, less demand for shops; may lower house prices; car sales firms move out; reduces labour mobility.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two characteristics of money.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: generally acceptable; portable; recognisable; divisible; durable; limited in supply; uniform. Accept an explanation e.g. 'easy to carry'. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two reasons why a reduction in their working hours may not cause public sector workers to move to working in the private sector.
questions.ms: 1 mark per reason + 1 per explanation. Public sector wages may still be higher (1) can buy more (1); better fringe benefits (1) e.g. pensions (1); more leisure time (1) better work-life balance (1); more job security (1) few private sector jobs (1); skills not transferable (1) occupational immobility (1); better working conditions (1); pay may not fall with hours (1). Consider first three only.

questions.text: Analyse how advances in technology could affect firms' profits.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Better capital goods (1) higher productivity (1) more output / lower costs (1) more profit (1). Better products / new products (1) more demand and revenue (1). New products may cut demand for related products (1) e.g. electric cars vs diesel (1). Online training (1) faster skills development (1). Internet / social media reach more customers abroad (1) more revenue (1). High initial cost of new technology (1) lowers profit short run (1). Small firms may be forced out (1) by the cost of technology (1). Reward lower costs once only.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a decrease in government spending will increase unemployment.
questions.ms:
Might: cuts to education / training reduce skills and productivity, raising structural unemployment; cuts to public sector wages may cause resignations; less spending on job vacancy information raises frictional unemployment; lower total demand causes cyclical unemployment.
Might not: lower inflation makes products more competitive, raising net exports; cutting unemployment benefits may reduce frictional unemployment; allows tax cuts that boost spending and investment; spending may be more effective e.g. training targeted at vacancies.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Define Consumer Prices Index.
questions.ms: A measure of inflation / the cost of living (1) using a weighted basket of goods and services (1).

questions.text: Explain two ways a government could intervene to reduce market failure.
questions.ms: 1 mark per way + 1 per explanation. Subsidise merit goods (1) to encourage consumption (1); tax demerit goods (1) to discourage consumption (1); maximum price on merit goods (1) / minimum price on demerit goods (1); provide public goods (1) as private firms won't (1); regulate monopolies (1) to stop abuse of market power (1); information campaigns / education (1) to raise awareness (1); training (1) to increase labour mobility (1). Consider first three only.

questions.text: Analyse how an increase in a country's foreign exchange rate could reduce inflation.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Appreciation (1) raises export prices (1) lowers import prices (1). Net exports fall (1) and exports are part of total demand (1) reducing demand-pull inflation (1). Cheaper imports put pressure on firms to keep prices low (1); cheaper imported raw materials (1) lower production costs (1) reducing cost-push inflation (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not an increase in a country's economic growth rate will reduce emigration from the country.
questions.ms:
Might: more employment; people won't need to seek jobs abroad; higher incomes / less poverty; more tax revenue for education and healthcare.
Might not: incomes may still be low; income may be unevenly distributed; people may not expect growth to last; growth and jobs may be better in other countries; more pollution / external costs; growth may bring worse working conditions; people emigrate for other reasons.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: What is the cause of scarcity in an economy?
questions.ms: Answer: D (unlimited wants)
questions.subtopic: 1.1 The nature of the basic economic problem

questions.text: What does a point on a production possibility curve for an economy represent?
options: maximum output possible with current technology
total demand for goods and services
questions.ms: Answer: C (maximum output possible with current technology)

questions.text: What is most likely to increase enterprise as a factor of production in an economy?
options: a decrease in government spending on education
a decrease in regulation on firms
an increase in taxation on firms
questions.ms: Answer: B (a decrease in regulation on firms)

questions.text: Which economic activity would be classified as macroeconomics?
options: households spend less on holidays abroad
income tax is increased by the government
world coffee price rises due to poor weather
questions.ms: Answer: B (income tax is increased by the government)

questions.text:
The diagram shows the effect of a decrease in price on the demand for a product.
What does the arrow on the diagram illustrate?
questions.ms: Answer: C (extension in demand)

questions.text: What is the correct formula to calculate price elasticity of supply?
options: the percentage change in price divided by the change in quantity supplied
the percentage change in price divided by the percentage change in quantity supplied
the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the change in price
the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price
questions.ms: Answer: D (the percentage change in quantity supplied divided by the percentage change in price)

questions.text: What is the most likely cause of a product having a price elasticity of demand greater than one?
options: The product has a close substitute.
The product is a habit-forming good.
The product requires only a small proportion of consumer income.
questions.ms: Answer: A (The product has a close substitute.)

questions.text:
For some illnesses, wearing a face mask has a benefit as it could prevent people from getting infected. Not all people are willing to wear face masks.
Based on the statement above, why would there be an inefficient allocation of face masks in the free market?
options: Consumers in the free market only consider private costs and benefits.
Face masks are non-rival and non-excludable.
There is abuse of monopoly power by the producer of face masks.
There is perfect information in the free market.
questions.ms: Answer: A (Consumers in the free market only consider private costs and benefits.)

questions.text: What would bring about a movement upwards along the supply curve for rice?
options: a decrease in the productivity of farmworkers
a decrease in the profitability of rice production
questions.ms: Answer: C (an increase in consumers’ incomes)

questions.text:
A government decides to reduce air pollution in city centres by giving financial assistance to bus companies, reducing their costs of production and prices for passengers.
Which type of policy measure is this?
questions.ms: Answer: C (a subsidy)

questions.text: What would be least likely to act as a store of value during a period of rapid inflation?
questions.ms: Answer: A (cash)

questions.text:
A country’s central bank raised the rate of interest from 1% to 4% per year.
How would this change have affected the amount saved and the cost of borrowing by individuals?
(amount saved | cost of borrowing)
questions.ms: Answer: D (increased | increased)

questions.text: Which factor would not increase the bargaining strength of a trade union to raise wages?
options: high union membership in the industry
questions.ms: Answer: C (legislation limiting strike action)

questions.text:
Which conditions are most likely to attract small firms to enter a market?
(the market for the product | fixed costs of entering the industry)
questions.ms: Answer: B (local | low)

questions.text:
The diagram shows a firm’s total cost (TC) curve.
What is the average variable cost if the firm produces 10 units of output?
questions.ms: Answer: A ($4)

questions.text:
The table shows the units of factors of production that a firm needs to employ for two different levels of output.
What is the firm experiencing?
questions.ms: Answer: B (diseconomies of scale)

questions.text: What is an example of a government macroeconomic aim?
options: a minimum of 10 years of schooling
a sales tax of 10% on consumer goods
questions.ms: Answer: C (a target rate of 2% inflation)

questions.text:
Government policy measures can affect economic activity in a country.
Which pair of monetary policy measures would be likely to increase employment?
options: depreciate foreign exchange rates and increase education spending
increase money supply and reduce interest rates
provide subsidies and grants and lower sales tax
reduce income tax and improve infrastructure
questions.ms: Answer: B (increase money supply and reduce interest rates)

questions.text: What would be most likely to encourage saving?
options: a rise in the exchange rate
a rise in the goods and services tax rate
a rise in the income tax rate
a rise in the interest rate
questions.ms: Answer: D (a rise in the interest rate)

questions.text:
The government of a country operating at full employment increases its spending on education and training.
How does this affect the likelihood of achieving low inflation in the short run and the long run?
(short run | long run)
questions.ms: Answer: B (less likely | more likely)

questions.text:
A government has introduced a tax on a necessity. Producers have passed on a large proportion of this tax to consumers in the form of higher prices.
Which row is correct?
(type of tax | price elasticity of demand)
questions.ms: Answer: D (indirect | price inelastic)

questions.text: What is most likely to lead to an increase in structural unemployment in a country?
options: The country is experiencing a period of negative economic growth.
The country is experiencing a period of positive economic growth.
The country is moving from producing primary sector goods to secondary sector goods.
The country is moving towards more flexible labour markets.
questions.ms: Answer: C (The country is moving from producing primary sector goods to secondary sector goods.)

questions.text: Which citizens are most likely to benefit in a period of rapid inflation?
options: citizens who are receiving fixed state benefits
citizens who have lent money at a fixed rate of interest
citizens who have borrowed money at a fixed rate of interest
questions.ms: Answer: D (citizens who have borrowed money at a fixed rate of interest)

questions.text: Which statement is correct about the Human Development Index (HDI) and real GDP?
options: HDI includes exports and imports while real GDP does not.
HDI includes life expectancy and years of schooling while real GDP does not.
HDI includes the level of output while real GDP does not.
HDI includes the level of unemployment in the population while real GDP does not.
questions.ms: Answer: B (HDI includes life expectancy and years of schooling while real GDP does not.)

questions.text: Other things being equal, what will cause a population both to increase and to age?
options: a fall in the birth rate
a fall in the death rate
a rise in both the birth rate and the death rate
a rise in the death rate and a fall in the birth rate
questions.ms: Answer: B (a fall in the death rate)

questions.text: Which change would be unlikely to be found in a country as it develops?
options: an increase in average incomes and a decrease in unemployment
an increase in manufacturing production and an increase in shipping services
an increase in subsistence farming and a decrease in financial services
an increase in tourism and an increase in the export of agricultural products
questions.ms: Answer: C (an increase in subsistence farming and a decrease in financial services)
questions.subtopic: 5.4 Differences in economic development between countries

questions.text:
It is cheaper for developed economies to buy some cereals from developing economies than to produce them domestically.
What might reduce international trade in cereals?
options: Cereals become less popular with the population of developing economies.
Developed economies place an embargo on cereal imports to prevent disease.
Governments tax cereal production in developed economies.
Producers of cereals in developing economies are subsidised.
questions.ms: Answer: B (Developed economies place an embargo on cereal imports to prevent disease.)

questions.text:
A country imposes a quota on imported cars.
What is the most likely outcome of this action?
options: a decrease in the domestic output of cars
a decrease in the domestic price of cars
an increase in the tax revenue from car imports
an increase in the total revenue of domestic car producers
questions.ms: Answer: D (an increase in the total revenue of domestic car producers)

questions.text:
An Argentine product initially sells in the US for $50 when the exchange rate between the two countries is 5 pesos to 1 dollar.
The exchange rate changes to 10 pesos to 1 dollar and the price of the product remains unchanged in Argentina.
What will be the new price of the product in the US?
questions.ms: Answer: B ($25)

questions.text: Which policy measure is most likely to reduce the current account deficit of the balance of payments of an economy?
options: decrease the level of subsidies to domestic producers
increase infrastructure spending to increase domestic productivity
questions.ms: Answer: B (increase infrastructure spending to increase domestic productivity)
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text: What is part of the economic definition of scarcity?
questions.ms: Answer: D (unlimited consumer wants)
questions.subtopic: 1.1 The nature of the basic economic problem

questions.text:
A country’s production possibility curve (PPC) moves from PPC1 to PPC2.
What could cause this movement in the PPC?
(better education | higher investment | lower unemployment)
questions.ms: Answer: D (true | true | false)

questions.text:
A government spends $100m on subsidising wind farm construction instead of spending it on an increase in healthcare.
Which economic concept does this spending decision illustrate?
questions.ms: Answer: D (opportunity cost)

questions.text: What is an example of a macroeconomic indicator?
options: average earnings in the secondary sector
total costs of German pharmaceutical firms
questions.ms: Answer: C (real Gross Domestic Product (real GDP))

questions.text:
Good X is demanded in two areas, Y and Z. The table shows the amount of X demanded in these areas at different prices.
What can be concluded from the table?
options: Consumers in area Y are more willing and able than consumers in area Z to buy good X.
Consumers in area Y are richer than consumers in area Z.
Consumers in area Y want the good more than consumers in area Z.
There are more consumers living in area Y than in area Z.
questions.ms: Answer: A (Consumers in area Y are more willing and able than consumers in area Z to buy good X.)

questions.text: Which price elasticity of demand (PED) would cause an increase in total revenue if the price of the good increased?
questions.ms: Answer: C (relatively inelastic)

questions.text:
The diagram shows the supply curve for coffee.
The price of coffee increases from P1 to P2.
How would this benefit firms in the coffee industry?
options: A higher price gives firms the ability to increase profits.
A higher price gives firms the incentive to reduce total fixed costs.
A higher price will encourage consumers to buy more coffee increasing total revenue.
A higher price will encourage less firms to enter the market to supply coffee.
questions.ms: Answer: A (A higher price gives firms the ability to increase profits.)

questions.text: What might be an external benefit of an increase in the number of university graduates in an economy?
options: an increase in revenue for the universities from fee-paying students
an increase in tax revenue from a more productive labour force
an increase in graduate employment as a percentage of the working population
an increase in wages for graduates
questions.ms: Answer: B (an increase in tax revenue from a more productive labour force)

questions.text:
The price of a good increases.
What could cause this?
options: The cost of raw materials falls.
The price of a complement rises.
The price of a substitute falls.
questions.ms: Answer: B (The incomes of consumers rise.)

questions.text: Imposing a maximum price for a good is an example of which type of government policy?
questions.ms: Answer: C (regulation)

questions.text:
Savers suffer as inflation rises to 4.4%.
Which function of money is most involved in this statement?
questions.ms: Answer: C (store of value)

questions.text:
One of the functions of money is to act as a measure of value.
What does this mean?
options: Money allows people to borrow and lend.
Money allows people to save their surplus income.
Money is used to buy goods and services.
Money is used to compare the worth of different goods and services.
questions.ms: Answer: D (Money is used to compare the worth of different goods and services.)

questions.text: Which trade union activity will be beneficial for firms?
options: balloting for industrial action to prevent redundancies
campaigning to raise wages of trade union members
instructing workers to strike over a safety dispute
providing training which raises productivity of workers
questions.ms: Answer: D (providing training which raises productivity of workers)

questions.text: What is not a variable cost of production?
options: extra pay for working additional hours
questions.ms: Answer: D (rent of offices)

questions.text: What is a definition of a firm’s revenue?
questions.ms: Answer: A (money received from sales)

questions.text: What could cause internal diseconomies of scale for a firm?
options: a fall in demand for the products produced by the firm
a merger with another firm that results in slower decision-making
spending more on research and development to create new products
the lack of skilled labour in the geographical area where the firm is based
questions.ms: Answer: B (a merger with another firm that results in slower decision-making)

questions.text:
A government decides to leave direct taxes unchanged but to increase indirect taxes.
What is this policy intended to achieve?
options: to increase the value of the exchange rate
to redistribute income from higher to lower income groups
to reduce the rate of inflation
questions.ms: Answer: C (to reduce a budget deficit)

questions.text: What is the most likely reason to increase government subsidies?
options: to decrease consumption of a merit good
to increase consumption of a merit good
to decrease consumption of a demerit good
to increase consumption of a demerit good
questions.ms: Answer: B (to increase consumption of a merit good)

questions.text: Which people are most likely to gain at a time of inflation?
options: those who are repaying borrowed money
questions.ms: Answer: D (those who are repaying borrowed money)

questions.text:
The government of country Z announces an increase in spending on work-place training.
What is the effect of this supply-side policy likely to be?
options: a decrease in country Z’s employment rate
a decrease in country Z’s exchange rate
an increase in country Z’s economic growth rate
an increase in country Z’s interest rate
questions.ms: Answer: C (an increase in country Z’s economic growth rate)

questions.text:
The table shows real GDP in US$ billion for a country over a three-year period.
What does the GDP data indicate for the country between year 1 and year 3?
options: a reduction in the rate of inflation
an increase in the rate of economic growth
the existence of economic growth per capita
questions.ms: Answer: C (the existence of economic growth)

questions.text: What is a likely consequence of a falling level of unemployment?
questions.ms: Answer: D (rise in income tax revenue)

questions.text:
The diagrams show Italy’s unemployment rate and GDP per head.
When do Italy’s unemployment rate and GDP per head rise at the same time?

During a recession, many people in a city become unemployed and their incomes fall. Some people can no longer pay the rent on their houses or buy the food they need.
What is the effect of the recession in the city?
(absolute poverty | relative poverty)
questions.ms: Answer: A (increases | increases)

questions.text:
The Peruvian government set itself the target of reducing the number of its population in poverty.
What change does not indicate that the Peruvian government had made progress towards this target?
options: a rise in the level of adult literacy
questions.ms: Answer: B (a rise in infant mortality)

questions.text: What is not a reason for the decline in manufacturing industries in developed economies in recent years?
options: growth of newly industrialised competitor countries
rising costs of factor inputs in the steel industry
considerable skill shortages as school-leavers prefer to work in the service sector
questions.ms: Answer: B (invention of automated production methods)
questions.subtopic: 5.4 Differences in economic development between countries

questions.text:
The table shows a country’s exports and imports.
What was the country’s balance of trade in goods and services?
questions.ms: Answer: C (a surplus of $7 million)
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text:
Country X exports steel to country Y at a price below its cost of production. This has led to a fall in demand for steel produced in country Y.
What is a method of trade protection that country Y could use to reduce the imports of steel from country X?
questions.ms: Answer: A (apply anti-dumping tariffs)

questions.text: What would increase the demand for a country’s currency on the foreign exchange market?
options: a decrease in its inward investment
a decrease in its rate of interest
questions.ms: Answer: C (an increase in its exports)

questions.text:
Country X has a persistent deficit on the current account of the balance payments.
Which policy measure is most likely to improve this situation?
questions.ms: Answer: A (lowering import quotas)
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text:
GDP per capita in Switzerland is high.
What is the reason why Swiss citizens still face the basic economic problem?
options: Income in Switzerland is unevenly distributed.
Swiss citizens expect high living standards.
Swiss citizens have to make choices in consumption.
questions.ms: Answer: D (Swiss citizens have to make choices in consumption.)
questions.subtopic: 1.1 The nature of the basic economic problem

questions.text:
The production possibility curve of a country has shifted from PPC1 to PPC2.
What could have caused this shift?
options: a decrease in the rate of unemployment
a fall in the birth rate
questions.ms: Answer: C (improved education)

questions.text: What is most likely to increase the geographical mobility of labour?
options: an increase in the amount of credit available to firms
an increase in the quantity of low-cost housing
an increase in spending by firms on research and development
an increase in spending by government on apprenticeships and training
questions.ms: Answer: B (an increase in the quantity of low-cost housing)

questions.text: What is not a microeconomic decision?
options: A firm decides to increase the price of its product.
A government decides to increase interest rates.
A household decides to reduce its demand for fuel.
A trade union decides to go on strike.
questions.ms: Answer: B (A government decides to increase interest rates.)

questions.text: What is a feature of a market in equilibrium?
options: there will be a surplus of products
questions.ms: Answer: C (the market will clear)

questions.text:
The diagram shows the supply curve for a good.
What is the name and cause of the movement from X to Y?
options: a contraction of supply caused by a decrease in demand
a contraction of supply caused by an increase in demand
an extension of supply caused by a decrease in demand
an extension of supply caused by an increase in demand
questions.ms: Answer: D (an extension of supply caused by an increase in demand)

questions.text: In the diagram, which supply curve has the perfectly inelastic supply?

The diagram shows the market for petrol (gasoline). SP is the supply of petrol based on the private cost of petrol production and SS is the supply of petrol based on the social cost of production.
Which distance shows the market failure caused by the production of petrol?
questions.ms: Answer: C (Q2 Q1)

questions.text:
In a given year, the world output of coal was 3.94 billion metric tonnes at an average yearly price of $252 per metric tonne.

What might have caused such a fall in the price of coal?
options: almost half the world’s coal reserves were in just two countries
the exhaustion of coal seams throughout the world
the switch to renewable sources of energy
the use of coal as a raw material as well as a fuel
questions.ms: Answer: C (the switch to renewable sources of energy)

questions.text:
A government believes that people eat too much sugar but not enough fruit.
