options: increase its tax | increase its tax
increase its tax | subsidise its production
subsidise its production | increase its tax
subsidise its production | subsidise its production
questions.ms: Answer: B (increase its tax | subsidise its production)

questions.text:
Which row shows a characteristic of money and a function of money?
(characteristic | function)
questions.ms: Answer: A (acceptability | medium of exchange)

questions.text: When will a central bank act as lender of last resort to a commercial bank?
options: when a commercial bank faces a liquidity crisis
when a commercial bank fails to make a profit
when a commercial bank needs to raise share capital
when a commercial bank reduces its lending rates
questions.ms: Answer: A (when a commercial bank faces a liquidity crisis)

questions.text: What is likely to increase the bargaining power of a trade union?
options: when the economy is experiencing rising cyclical unemployment
when the labour market moves from long-term to short-term contracts of employment
when the price elasticity of demand for the product is price-elastic
when the trade union supplies all the labour required by the employer
questions.ms: Answer: D (when the trade union supplies all the labour required by the employer)

questions.text: What is a likely reason why firms do not grow in size?
options: External diseconomies of scale occur at high levels of output.
Internal economies of scale occur at high levels of output.
Internal economies of scale occur at low levels of output.
Internal diseconomies of scale occur at low levels of output.
questions.ms: Answer: D (Internal diseconomies of scale occur at low levels of output.)

questions.text:
The table shows the activities of four firms.
Which combination of firms would be an example of horizontal integration?
questions.ms: Answer: B (1 and 3)

questions.text: What is a reason why firms making similar products sometimes locate near each other?
options: There are external economies of scale.
There are internal economies of scale.
questions.ms: Answer: B (There are external economies of scale.)

questions.text:
A government wishes to increase its spending on public goods.
Which sector should have a spending increase to achieve this?
questions.ms: Answer: C (national defence)

questions.text: Which government measure would lead directly to more exports of goods?
options: a restriction of bank credit creation
an increase in the rate of interest
the issue of more bank notes and coins
questions.ms: Answer: A (a devaluation of the currency)

questions.text:
A government wishes to stimulate economic recovery.
Which action will assist this?
questions.ms: Answer: B (decreasing income tax)

questions.text: What is the most likely effect on an economy of a successful supply-side policy?
options: an increase in the general price level
an increase in the interest rate
an increase in the money supply
an increase in the potential GDP
questions.ms: Answer: D (an increase in the potential GDP)

questions.text:
A country is experiencing high economic growth caused by an increase in consumer spending.
What are the most likely effects on inflation and unemployment?
questions.ms: Answer: C (inflation rises and unemployment falls)

questions.text: Which pair is most likely to be provided by the private sector in a mixed economy?
questions.ms: Answer: C (insurance and banks)

questions.text:
An economy is experiencing a sustained fall in the general price level.
Which term is used to describe this?
questions.ms: Answer: A (deflation)

questions.text: What is most likely to cause an increase in relative poverty?
options: an increase in the national minimum wage
pension increases below the rate of inflation
questions.ms: Answer: C (pension increases below the rate of inflation)

questions.text: What might explain the high population growth in some developing countries?
options: high birth rates and falling death rates
falling birth rates and rising death rates
questions.ms: Answer: A (high birth rates and falling death rates)

questions.text: Which combination of factors might cause a country to be classified as developing rather than developed?
options: a government budget deficit and a low death rate
a high birth rate and a low death rate
a large population and a current account deficit
a poor education system and a low standard of living
questions.ms: Answer: D (a poor education system and a low standard of living)
questions.subtopic: 5.4 Differences in economic development between countries

questions.text: What is certain to encourage a higher level of international trade?
options: conservation of resources and unstable exchange rates
exploitation of resources and wider use of quotas
increased support for home industries and increased tariffs
more specialisation and falling transport costs
questions.ms: Answer: D (more specialisation and falling transport costs)

questions.text:
The import of a product from another country has been banned.
Which term describes this method of protection?
questions.ms: Answer: A (embargo)

questions.text:
A developing country’s two major sources of income from international trade are fishing and tourism.
If the country’s exchange rate depreciated, what is likely to happen?
options: Imported goods would become cheaper for local people.
The country would definitely become poorer.
The price of fish sold as exports would become cheaper.
Tourists to the country would be discouraged by higher prices.
questions.ms: Answer: C (The price of fish sold as exports would become cheaper.)

questions.text: What is the correct formula for calculating the current account of the balance of payments?
options: balance of trade in goods + balance of trade in services + primary income balance + secondary income balance
government revenue from abroad – domestic government spending
percentage change in quantity demanded of exports ÷ percentage change in price of imports
total exports of services + total imports of goods
questions.ms: Answer: A (balance of trade in goods + balance of trade in services + primary income balance + secondary income balance)
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text: Calculate Australia's unemployment rate in 2021.
questions.ms: 1 mark: 4% (0.56 / 14 × 100). Allow 4 without the % sign.

questions.text: Identify two substitutes for coal.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: gas; offshore wind / wind power; solar power / panels.

questions.text: Explain one economy of scale that could benefit a coal-mining firm.
questions.ms: 1 mark identification + 1 mark explanation. Managerial / labour economy (1) employing specialist workers e.g. mining engineers (1). OR Technical economy (1) using efficient, technologically advanced equipment e.g. drones (1). OR External economy of scale (1) e.g. a skilled labour force (1).

questions.text: Explain two influences on the price elasticity of supply of coal.
questions.ms: 1 mark per influence + 1 per explanation. Storage (1) expensive to store, so supply is inelastic (1). Time to build a new mine / production time (1) takes a long time, so supply is inelastic (1). Stocks (1) may make supply elastic (1).

questions.text: Draw a demand and supply diagram to show how setting a maximum price below the equilibrium price will affect a market.
questions.ms: 1 mark each: axes labelled price and quantity (1); demand and supply curves labelled (1); price line set BELOW equilibrium (1); demand shown greater than supply at that price, e.g. two dotted lines down to the quantity axis (1). Accept a correctly labelled shortage. No mark for demand > supply if the curves are drawn wrongly.

questions.text: Analyse whether large coal-producing countries are likely to be net exporters of coal.
questions.ms: Expected outcome: large producers may have a surplus to sell abroad (1); most of the evidence supports this (1). Evidence: five of the seven countries consume less coal than they produce (1); a calculation e.g. Australia could have exported 394 million tonnes (1). Analysis: producers with surplus coal may gain economies of scale / have low prices so can export (1). Exception: China or India (1) consumed more than they produced (1). Analysis of exception: they may be net importers (1) as a developing country needing more energy / used up stocks (1); countries may both import and export coal (1). Max 5.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not an increase in the size of its coal industry will benefit the Australian economy.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for might, up to 4 for might not, max 6.
Might: higher GDP / growth (1) higher living standards / incomes (1); less unemployment (1) structural unemployment (1); better current account (1) as Australia is a net exporter of coal (1); more tax revenue (1) so more government spending (1); economies of scale (1) lower prices for households and industry (1).
Might not: more pollution (1) health problems / lower living standards (1) less tourism (1); other forms of power may not be developed (1) example (1); workers may leave jobs with better conditions (1); mining is dangerous (1) lower life expectancy / illness (1); global demand for coal may fall (1) leaving unsold stocks (1); stocks of coal depleted quickly (1) so fewer exports later (1) and less employment (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not Australia is likely to have a budget deficit in 2026.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for likely, up to 4 for not likely, max 6.
Likely: unemployment forecast to rise (1) more spent on benefits (1) less income tax revenue (1); more spending on retraining (1); larger population needs more spending (1) e.g. pensions, healthcare, education (1); deficits in previous years mean interest must be paid on the debt (1).
Not likely: population and labour force forecast to rise (1) more taxpayers / fewer claiming benefits (1); tax revenue may rise (1) from higher profits / tax rates (1); GDP forecast to rise (1) more people in work (1) more direct and indirect tax revenue (1); state support for industries may fall (1) as it may have been high in 2021 due to Covid-19 (1).

questions.text: Identify two functions of money.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: medium of exchange; unit of account / measure of value; store of value; standard of deferred payment. A description without the term gets the mark. Nothing for characteristics of money. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain how improved education may affect the demand for cigarettes and for fresh fruit.
questions.ms: Demand for cigarettes may fall (1) as people are better informed about harmful effects / cigarettes are a demerit good (1). Demand for fresh fruit may rise (1) as people are better informed about its benefits / it's a merit good / better paid jobs mean they can afford it (1). Only accept higher demand for cigarettes if linked to higher income from education.

questions.text: Analyse the causes of an increase in a government's tax revenue.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Tax revenue is government income / part of fiscal policy (1) spent on objectives e.g. education (1). More employment (1) more income (1) higher income tax revenue (1). More spending (1) higher indirect tax revenue (1). Higher profits (1) more corporation tax (1). Larger population (1) more taxpayers (1). Higher tax rates (1) raise revenue without any change in income / spending (1); lower rates may cut avoidance / evasion (1) and raise incentives (1). Better tax collection (1) less corruption / simpler forms (1). Wider tax base (1). More imports (1) more tariff revenue (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not an increase in unemployment benefit payments would reduce poverty.
questions.ms:
Might: raises incomes of those on low incomes; they can buy more basic necessities; may reduce absolute poverty; raises total demand, which may reduce unemployment; lets people seek education and become more employable.
Might not: may be a disincentive to find work; people may become dependent on benefits; doesn't help all those on low incomes e.g. the retired and the sick; may not reduce relative poverty; some unemployed may not claim; opportunity cost, spending on e.g. education might work better; benefit may be small or rise less than inflation.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two reasons why death rates may vary between countries.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2, differences in: income / living standards; healthcare; education; nutrition; lifestyles; average age; infectious diseases; war / conflict; natural disasters; pollution; working conditions; crime. Not population size (affects number, not rate). Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two causes of an increase in the size of a country's labour force.
questions.ms: 1 mark per cause + 1 per explanation. Higher birth rate (1) more people of working age in the long run (1); immigration (1) many immigrants are of working age (1); higher retirement age (1) people work longer (1); lower school leaving age (1); lower death rate / longer life expectancy (1) fewer die before retirement (1); social change (1) more women working (1); higher wages (1) attract people back into the labour market (1).

questions.text: Analyse how an increase in labour productivity in a country can increase a surplus on the current account of its balance of payments.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Output per worker rises (1) lowering average costs (1) and prices (1) / raising export quality (1). Exports become more internationally competitive (1) demand for exports rises (1) export revenue rises (1). Imports become relatively dearer / lower quality (1) less competitive (1) demand for imports falls (1) import spending falls (1). More output (1) allows more exports (1) and fewer imports (1).
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text: Discuss why some countries may experience lower inflation in the future and some may not.
questions.ms:
Why some might: new technology may cut production costs; better education and healthcare could raise labour productivity; globalisation may increase international competition; trade union power may fall, lowering wage rises; successful government policy e.g. reducing demand.
Why some might not: consumers may become optimistic and spend more; governments may increase their spending; interest rates may fall; total demand may rise; raw materials may run out; rising energy and food prices.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two influences on which country a person decides to work in.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: wages / GDP per head; working conditions; job opportunities / security; qualifications required; family ties; language; immigration restrictions; personal safety; living standards / cost of living; welfare, healthcare and education provision. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain, with examples, the difference between a merit good and a public good.
questions.ms: Merit good e.g. education / fruit (1) is beneficial, under-consumed as people are unaware of its benefits, so underproduced without government intervention (1). Public good e.g. defence / street lighting / police / sea defences (1) would not be produced by the private sector, non-rival and non-excludable, so financed by government (1).

questions.text: Analyse how an increase in government spending could increase life expectancy.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis. More spending on: healthcare (1) better quality / access to healthcare (1); education (1) healthier lifestyles (1) more exercise (1) better nutrition (1); benefits (1) access to basic necessities / less poverty (1); green energy (1) less pollution (1); infrastructure (1) fewer traffic accidents (1) less congestion and stress (1); police (1) fewer deaths through crime (1); more spending overall (1) more employment and income (1). Max 3 for just listing areas; max 4 if only one area is analysed.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a rise in a country's foreign exchange rate would benefit its economy.
questions.ms:
Might: cheaper imports; lower inflation as raw material costs fall and firms face more competitive pressure; can buy more imports for any given quantity of exports; could reduce a current account surplus, allowing more products to be consumed.
Might not: dearer exports; fewer exports and less export revenue; lower economic growth; higher unemployment; could increase a current account deficit.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two reasons why rich households spend more than the average household.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: higher incomes; easier to borrow; more confidence; more savings / wealth; high cost of luxury goods; showing status; larger families. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain the significance of a production point inside a PPC and a production point on its PPC.
questions.ms: Point inside the PPC: output is lower than possible (1) as there are unemployed resources / inefficient use of resources (1). Point on the PPC: output is at its maximum (1) as all resources are employed efficiently (1). Also accept: a production point shows a combination of goods produced (1) with an example (1).

questions.text: Analyse why someone who has been unemployed for more than a year may not get another job.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. May lose skills (1) qualifications go out of date (1) ill-health (1) lack of recent experience (1) costly to retrain (1) less attractive to employers (1). Industry in decline (1) needs retraining (1). Economy in recession (1) few vacancies (1). Loss of confidence / discouraged (1) less effort job hunting (1). Occupationally (1) or geographically immobile (1). Benefits may be higher than low wages (1). Discrimination (1) e.g. age (1). May retire (1) and leave the labour force (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a government should encourage firms to merge.
questions.ms:
Should: economies of scale; lower average costs; lower prices for consumers; better quality products; more internationally competitive, improving the current account; higher profits mean more corporation tax.
Should not: diseconomies of scale; more monopoly power / less competition; higher prices; less innovation; rationalisation may mean job losses; should be left to market forces.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Calculate the number of people who were living in poverty in Guyana in 2020.
Identify two causes of the decrease in the output of sugar in 2020.
questions.ms: 1 mark each: bad weather; falling (global) demand. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain how economic growth is measured.
questions.ms: Real (1) GDP / national output / income / expenditure (1). GDP per head is not accepted for GDP.

questions.text: Explain two reasons why labour mobility may increase in Guyana in the future.
questions.ms: 1 mark per reason + 1 per explanation. More spending on education (1) better skills, more occupational mobility (1). Better / cheaper rail travel / infrastructure (1) easier to work further away, more geographical mobility (1). Better internet access (1) people learn new skills / find out about job opportunities (1). Net immigration (1) migrants may be skilled / more willing to move around the country (1). Consider first three only.

questions.text: Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effect of a decrease in the price of rail transport on the market for car transport.
questions.ms: 1 mark each: axes labelled price and quantity (1); original demand and supply curves labelled (1); DEMAND curve shifts LEFT (1); equilibria shown P1/Q1 and P2/Q2 or E1/E2 (1).

questions.text: Analyse the relationship between GDP per head and internet access.
questions.ms: Expected relationship: direct / positive (1) higher GDP per head, higher internet access (1). Evidence (must compare, up to 2): Iceland has the highest GDP per head and highest internet access; Eritrea the lowest of both; France second highest of both. Analysis: higher GDP per head means households can afford internet / more tax revenue to fund provision / internet access raises productivity and wages (up to 2). Exception: Guyana / Morocco (1) e.g. Guyana has higher GDP per head but low internet access (1). Analysis of exception: other influences e.g. education levels (1). No marks for just repeating figures. Max 5.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not the discovery of oil is likely to increase living standards in Guyana.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for likely, up to 4 for not likely, max 6.
Likely: more exports (1) economic growth (1) higher incomes / GDP per head (1) can buy more goods and necessities (1) less poverty (1); creates jobs (1) less emigration / more immigration (1); more tax revenue (1) to spend on e.g. education and healthcare (1); MNC may improve infrastructure / training (1).
Not likely: pollution / external costs / environmental damage (1) harming health / life expectancy (1); poor working conditions (1); MNC may send profits home (1) drive out domestic firms (1) deplete oil reserves (1); MNC may employ its own country's workers (1); global demand for oil may fall / overdependence on oil / trade restrictions (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not Guyana would benefit from an increase in the size of its population.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for would, up to 4 for would not, max 6.
Would: population is below the optimum (1) so resources used better (1); immigration (1) brings new ideas, skills, technology (1); bigger labour force (1) if more people of working age (1) more tax revenue (1) for education and healthcare (1); more consumer spending (1) higher total demand (1); more output / growth (1); lower dependency ratio (1).
Would not: pollution / congestion / overcrowding (1) environmental damage (1); if from a lower death rate / higher birth rate, more young or old people (1) higher dependency ratio (1); extra people may be unemployed (1); pressure on housing / welfare (1) more government spending needed (1); inflation (1); possible overpopulation (1) resources depleted faster (1).

questions.text: Identify two influences, other than price, on a customer's choice of bank.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: services provided; amount willing to lend; size of bank; online facilities; location; interest paid or charged; where family banks; advertising; green investments; community involvement; reputation; confidence / safety; relationship with staff; foreign currency exchange; Islamic banking. Not brand loyalty. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two reasons why a merger may result in higher prices for consumers.
questions.ms: 1 mark per reason + 1 per explanation. More market power / less competition / monopoly (1) can raise price as consumers can't switch / demand more inelastic / becomes a price maker (1). Diseconomies of scale (1) higher average costs passed on in prices (1). The merger itself is expensive (1) prices raised to cover e.g. retraining / redundancy costs (1). Not 'higher costs because the firm is larger'. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Analyse how an increase in bank lending can benefit an economy.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. More consumer spending (1) higher total demand (1) more employment (1) less deflation (1). More investment in capital goods (1) new technology / innovation (1) higher productivity (1) better quality (1) lower prices (1) more exports (1) fewer imports (1) better current account (1) economic growth / firms expand or set up (1). People can improve skills / start small businesses / buy necessities (1). Loans to struggling firms (1) stop them closing (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a market economy allocates resources in the best possible way.
questions.ms:
Might: prices move to reflect changes in demand and supply; resources move from products falling in demand to those rising in demand; profit incentive to produce what consumers want (consumer sovereignty); competition drives efficiency, lowering costs and prices; wage changes move labour to the jobs most in demand.
Might not: merit goods under-consumed so too few resources go to them; demerit goods over-consumed; no resources go to public goods as there's no incentive; factor immobility; monopolies may restrict output; external costs and benefits ignored.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two objectives of private sector firms.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: profit (maximisation); growth / high sales; market share / dominance; survival; improving the environment / social welfare. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain one reason why the quantity of land may increase and one reason why the quality of land may increase.
questions.ms: Quantity (1 + 1): land reclamation (1) creating land from the sea (1); less overfishing / hunting (1) restoring stocks (1); less flooding (1) avoids soil erosion (1); discovery of new natural resources (1) e.g. oil (1). Quality (1 + 1): fertilisers (1) more fertile / productive land (1); less pollution (1) prevents damage (1); good weather (1); better equipment / technology (1) raises productivity of land (1).

questions.text: Analyse how an increase in investment may affect unemployment.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Spending on capital goods (1) raises total demand (1) firms expand / new firms set up / growth (1) more workers needed (1) reducing cyclical (1) unemployment (1). Investment in education / training / R&D (1) raises skills (1) and mobility (1) reducing structural unemployment (1). Infrastructure (1) raises geographical mobility (1). BUT capital may replace workers (1) production more capital-intensive (1) capital is a substitute for labour (1) technological unemployment (1). Credit rise / fall in unemployment once only.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a government should try to prevent a rise in unemployment.
questions.ms:
Should: keeps output / economic growth up; more tax revenue; less spending on unemployment benefit; protects living standards / avoids poverty.
Should not: unemployment may already be low; reducing unemployment may cause inflation; higher incomes may cause a current account deficit; some unemployment creates flexibility; opportunity cost of policy measures; government may have other objectives.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two reasons why a government may set an NMW.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: raise wages; reduce poverty / raise living standards; reduce income inequality; prevent exploitation / ensure fair wages; encourage job seeking; reduce emigration. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two causes of an increase in the value of a country's floating foreign exchange rate.
questions.ms: 1 mark per cause + 1 per explanation. Higher demand for the currency (1) from more exports / current account surplus (1) due to higher incomes abroad (1) lower inflation / better quality (1); more foreign investment (1); higher interest rates (1) attract hot money (1); speculation the currency will rise (1). Lower supply of the currency (1) fewer imports (1) lower incomes at home (1); domestic firms invest less abroad (1); lower interest rates abroad (1). Credit higher demand and lower supply once each.

questions.text: Analyse how an increase in the price of milk may affect the revenue earned by milk producers and soft drinks producers.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis. Demand for milk contracts (1). The effect on milk producers' revenue depends on PED (1): if elastic, revenue falls (1) as quantity falls by a bigger % than price rises (1); if inelastic, revenue rises (1) as quantity falls by a smaller % (1). Demand for soft drinks increases (1) so their producers' revenue rises (1) as soft drinks are a substitute for milk (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not small firms are more likely to go out of business than large firms.
questions.ms:
Might: high average costs; can't benefit from economies of scale; less likely to get bank loans; less retained profit; may be new, testing demand, with inexperienced entrepreneurs.
Might not: less likely to suffer diseconomies of scale; may get government financial help; customer loyalty; more flexible; may have a monopoly in a niche / specialist market.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify the opportunity cost of households spending their income and the opportunity cost of Chinese firms exporting goods and services.
questions.ms: Saving (1). Selling / consuming the products at home (1).

questions.text: Explain two reasons why some top sportspeople have high earnings.
questions.ms: 1 mark per reason + 1 per explanation. High / inelastic demand (1) large crowds / TV rights sold for large fees / merchandise and sponsorship generate high profits (1). Low / inelastic supply / few substitutes (1) high bargaining power / rare talent / years of training / experience / dangerous sports (1).

questions.text: Analyse the reasons for imposing tariffs on imports.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Improve the current account (1) imports dearer (1) less demand for imports / more net exports (1) higher total demand (1). Protect infant / declining / strategic industries (1) raise growth (1) and employment (1) as people switch to domestic products (1). Raise revenue (1) for e.g. education / to cut a budget deficit (1). Discourage harmful imports / demerit goods (1). Prevent dumping / unfair competition (1). Retaliation (1) against other countries' tariffs (1). Prevent a fall in the exchange rate (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not a country with a high economic growth rate will have a deficit on the current account of its balance of payments.
questions.ms:
Might: higher incomes mean more imports; firms switch products from foreign markets to the growing home market; firms import more raw materials and capital goods; inflation may reduce price competitiveness.
Might not: growth may be export-led; growth may encourage investment that raises quality and lowers prices; more tax revenue may fund education and healthcare, raising productivity; the country may impose trade restrictions / lower the exchange rate.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.
questions.subtopic: 6.4 Current account of the balance of payments

questions.text: Calculate New Zealand's GDP per head in 2020.
questions.ms: 1 mark: $39 000 ($195bn ÷ 5m). Accept without the $ sign.

questions.text: Identify two external costs arising from the milk and car industries.
questions.ms: 1 mark each: air pollution; damage to the environment where wild animals live. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain the impact on a cow farmer's profits if they are unable to find a different source of revenue.
questions.ms: Profit is revenue minus costs (1). Profits will fall (1) due to a lower quantity sold / lower supply (1). Less revenue (1) less income for farmers (1) farmers may become unemployed (1). Max 2.

questions.text: Explain the two plans that the New Zealand government has to reduce external costs to the environment.
questions.ms: 1 mark per plan + 1 per explanation. End imports of petrol-powered cars by 2032 (1) fewer petrol cars, less use of fossil fuels / an embargo / more electric cars used (1). Limit the number of cows each farmer can keep (1) less air pollution from cows / less habitat damage / regulation with fines (1).

questions.text: Draw a demand and supply diagram to show the effect of a cheaper substitute on the market for petrol-powered cars.
questions.ms: 1 mark each: axes labelled price and quantity (1); original demand and supply curves labelled (1); DEMAND curve shifts LEFT (1); equilibria shown P1/Q1 and P2/Q2 or E1/E2 (1).

questions.text: Analyse the relationship between a country's share of world GDP (%) and its share of world carbon dioxide emissions (%).
questions.ms: Expected relationship: positive (1) higher share of world GDP, higher share of emissions (1). Evidence (up to 2): New Zealand lowest in both; Thailand second lowest in both; China and the US highest two in both. Analysis: producing more output needs more factories, energy and transport, so more emissions (up to 2). Exception: China / US (1) China has the second highest share of GDP but the highest share of emissions (1). Analysis of exception: China has a larger secondary sector / more heavy industry / larger population (1). Max 5.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not an increase in exports of clean and green products will help the New Zealand government achieve its macroeconomic aims.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for will, up to 4 for won't, max 6.
Will: economic growth (1) as more exports raise total demand (1) green products may have higher demand (1) and higher prices (1); smaller current account deficit (1) as export value rises (1) more net exports (1); less unemployment (1) as more goods need more workers (1) less poverty (1); improved HDI (1).
Won't: not all firms benefit (1) less green firms lose revenue / profit (1) cut costs (1) hire fewer workers (1) more unemployment (1); higher total demand (1) causes inflation (1) as firms raise prices (1) lowering real incomes (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not job losses caused by a change to a carbon-neutral economy will be harmful.
questions.ms:
Up to 4 marks for harmful, up to 4 for not harmful, max 6.
Harmful: more poverty (1) less income (1) can't afford necessities (1) possible crime (1); losses for local firms that serve these communities (1) less local spending (1) firms may close (1); lost output (1) economy inside its PPC / unused resources (1); lost skills / motivation (1) occupational immobility (1) retraining costs (1); double effect on government finances (1) less tax (1) more benefits (1); unequal burden (1) structural unemployment (1) more inequality (1).
Not harmful: temporary (1) frictional unemployment (1) as green jobs are available (1); high factor mobility (1) workers move industries (1) with education / training (1); new jobs may pay more (1) boosting demand (1); better air quality (1) better health and productivity (1); less spent on healthcare (1) more for education / training (1).

questions.text: Identify two types of cost to a firm.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: total cost; average total cost; fixed cost; variable cost; average fixed cost; average variable cost. Accept any relevant cost e.g. labour cost, and abbreviations e.g. TC. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two roles of commercial banks for firms.
questions.ms: 1 mark per role + 1 per explanation. Loans / overdrafts / finance (1) to fund investment, expansion, start-up or day-to-day costs (1). Process payments (1) internet banking, transfers, card payments (1). Bank drafts / cheques (1). Safe place to keep money (1) deposits earn interest (1). Safekeeping of documents (1). Currency exchange (1) for international transactions (1). Insurance (1) reduces risk (1). Consider first three only.

questions.text: Analyse the causes of differences in the level of income between countries.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Productivity (1) workers produce more (1) and earn more (1). Natural resources (1) e.g. oil or gold (1). Population growth (1) more people to produce (1) lower labour costs (1) more investment (1). Sector mix / level of development (1) more secondary and tertiary output means more value added (1) less dependence on weather (1). Specialisation / exports (1). Minimum wage levels (1). Saving and investment (1) higher productivity growth (1). Education (1) more skills (1) higher output (1). Health / healthcare (1) healthier, more productive workers (1). Unemployment (1). Birth rates / ageing (1). War / natural disasters (1). Accept arguments for lower incomes.
questions.subtopic: 5.4 Differences in economic development between countries

questions.text: Discuss whether or not low tax rates benefit an economy.
questions.ms:
Might: low corporation tax encourages investment, raising productivity and growth, and demand for labour; low income tax encourages people into the labour force and raises disposable income, consumer spending and output; low indirect tax cuts production costs, reducing cost-push inflation and making exports more competitive (better current account).
Might not: less government revenue for public goods / infrastructure; more production means more pollution; low direct taxes may be inflationary and increase inequality; more trade means more pollution from transport; low tax on demerit goods may worsen health / market failure; low tariffs may worsen the current account.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Identify two challenges facing small firms.
questions.ms: 1 mark each, max 2: raising finance; can't employ specialist staff; less well known; managing cash flow; survival / high competition; no economies of scale / high average cost. Accept any reasonable challenge. Consider first three only.

questions.text: Explain two possible opportunity costs for firms if they invest in the latest technology.
questions.ms: 1 mark per opportunity cost + 1 per explanation. Can't pay as much in wages (1) forgo extra / more skilled workers (1). Lower quality raw materials (1) lower product quality (1). Can't afford a good location (1) harder for customers to reach (1). Can't buy land (1) for expansion (1). Less spending on advertising / marketing (1) forgo higher demand (1). Retained profits (1) could have gone to the owners (1). Consider first three only.

questions.text: Analyse two causes of a fall in demand for a product such as Chinese food.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis. Cheaper / better substitutes (1) demand switches to e.g. Indian food (1) more advertising of substitutes / rivals enter (1). Dearer complements (1) e.g. delivery charges (1). Lower incomes (1) people eat out less (1) as eating out is a luxury (1). Change in tastes / trends (1) towards other food (1). Lower quality (1) lack of investment (1) health reports favouring other food (1). Less advertising (1) less awareness (1). Consider first three causes only.

questions.text: Discuss whether or not competition is harmful to a firm.
questions.ms:
Harmful: lower market share; less revenue / profit; less growth; less reinvested profit so less innovation; may need to lower prices or spend more to compete; hard to enter or stay in an industry with large low-cost firms.
Not harmful: less complacency; more innovation; better quality goods and services; domestic competition builds international competitiveness.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.

questions.text: Define emigration.
questions.ms: People leaving (1) a country (1) to live in another country (1). Max 2.

questions.text: Explain two causes of a recession.
questions.ms: 1 mark per cause + 1 per explanation. Fall in total demand (1) from lower confidence / consumption / government spending / exports (1). Fall in investment (1) lower productive capacity (1). Falling population (1) e.g. emigration, fewer workers (1). War / natural disasters (1) destroy factors of production (1). Higher interest rates (1) less borrowing and spending (1). Lower confidence (1) capital flight (1). Higher income / corporation tax (1) less disposable income / investment (1). Lower productivity (1). Consider first three only.

questions.text: Analyse policy measures a government could use to attract workers to return to their home country.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Higher national minimum wage (1) attracts low-paid workers back (1). Expansionary fiscal / monetary policy (1) more job opportunities (1). Better education, healthcare, housing, pensions (1) higher living standards (1). Better working conditions / regulations protecting workers (1). Greater security (1). Labour market reforms (1) easier hiring, more jobs (1). Lower direct taxes (1) higher disposable income (1) incentive to return and work (1). Deregulation (1) more firms start up (1) people return to start businesses (1). Lower inflation (1) lower cost of living (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not an economy benefits from many of its students studying abroad.
questions.ms:
Might: better education abroad gives better skills / experience; higher productivity when they return; learn new technologies; build business contacts abroad; bring back new ideas / products; less poverty; further development; government spends less on education.
Might not: students may not return (brain drain); studying abroad is expensive, money flows out; only some can afford it, increasing inequality; domestic universities may not develop due to lack of demand; loss of consumption / growth at home; unemployment of teachers and lecturers, costing benefits. Not a problem if inflow of foreign students exceeds the outflow.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.
questions.subtopic: 5.4 Differences in economic development between countries

questions.text: Define government budget.
questions.ms: A plan / forecast (1) of government expenditure (1) and government revenue (1). Max 2.

questions.text: Explain, with examples, the difference between private benefits and external benefits.
questions.ms: Private benefits go to the consumers or producers of a product (1) e.g. a better job for someone who gets educated / profits a firm earns (1). External benefits go to third parties (1) e.g. higher productivity from a better educated workforce / better healthcare from better qualified doctors (1).

questions.text: Analyse the reasons why workers employed in education may earn more than workers employed in other industries.
questions.ms: Coherent analysis, 1 per point. Higher demand for education workers (1) as demand for education is higher (1) labour is a derived demand (1). Lower supply (1) fewer qualified people want to teach (1). Stronger bargaining power (1) strong trade unions (1). Less discrimination (1) pay based on productivity (1). Government spends more on education (1) sets higher wages (1) as education is essential (1). More skilled (1) long training (1) higher productivity (1). Tertiary workers earn more (1) more value added (1).

questions.text: Discuss whether or not having a large population is beneficial for the economy.
questions.ms:
Might: large labour supply, more productive capacity, PPC shifts out; more taxpayers to fund public services; high spending and total demand, high growth; firms invest more as profits are higher and workers easy to find; competition among workers raises quality / productivity; many entrepreneurs, more innovation; high demand lets firms gain economies of scale.
Might not: strain on resources e.g. housing, schools, hospitals; external costs e.g. pollution; high demand may cause demand-pull inflation; shortage of jobs, more unemployment; depends on the population's composition e.g. many under-5s won't raise output in the short run.
Levels: L3 (6-8) reasoned discussion of both sides, developed and evaluated; L2 (3-5) reasoned but may be one-sided or lack depth; L1 (1-2) simple use of terms.
